item.title: Memo: Firebell
item.description:
I’ve been sharing around a draft memo for a new project. Here I’m sharing it with you. This is a google doc version for commenting on, which is also copied below.

—

Memo: Firebell

Katja Grace, Nov 17 2026

Seeking: all feedback, questions, indications of whether you would join this or what would make a difference to that

I’m starting a thing (membership group?) called Firebell.

The basic idea:

  1. you join by endorsing a specific (TBD) statement that AI poses a dire threat to humanity, and that this is an emergency.

  2. Then you are metaphorically part of a giant human fire-alarm for AI. The call to action is to “make noise” aka spread the word, get more firebell members.

  3. Members can talk to each other in a private forum

  4. Members have a collection of guides for different ways to ‘make noise’. some abstract (dinners, talking to your family at thanksgiving, writing to friends, posting on social media, telling politicians), some involving physical bells (ring at 8pm every night across the city, ring outside labs when they step further into danger), some symbolic (bell earrings, tshirts). These are evolving, and members can add more, vote on them, discuss in the forum, help each other. Members are encouraged to send people back to the firebell website (firebell.ai)

  5. Possible gamified elements (track who brought in new members and have leaderboards, challenge people to do a thing each day from the list, etc)

Some key pieces of why I am especially excited for this vision:

Anchored around a simple statement thus minimizing possible message drift, and making policing of it simpler

Call to action is spreading the message / getting other people to join (aka endorse statement) not direct political goals

  • Lots of tractable and satisfying actions possible here (versus dearth of them for direct political ends)

  • Growing the set of people for whom this feels like an emergency is more important than pushing directly for policy stuff with the tiny set of people we have, is my guess

  • If the explicit goal is spreading the message, then spreading it feels like winning, whereas if explicit goal is a policy ask, spreading message feels ineffectual

  • The amount of tinder for a movement like this feels very high - people are somewhat concerned but not finding it salient, feel powerless and out of touch with ways to do anything

Social contact is a priority, versus just being on a list where a movement org contacts you sometimes. This is important because people nominally care about pausing AI, but it isn’t very salient, and I think social salience matters a lot here.

  • Members are immediately in an online forum together, where people are discussing what to do

  • Actions for spreading the word often involve real-life social component. E.g. discussion dinners for friends, talking to family, writing a social media post, watch parties for key pieces of media

Bells aka strong and fitting thematic concept

  • The group is a firebell: a big human fire alarm for AI, made of myriad people with bells

  • Bells are evocative, simple, concrete, wholesome, physical, only super annoying to 10% of people

  • Everyone understands that a fire alarm makes noise about a problem without having a particular solution in mind - it tells some people to get out of the building and others to come with hoses and others to grab buckets. It’s not a copout to pull a fire alarm without a specific plan.

  • There is a lot of scope for thematic actions - ringing bells in a posse outside labs when a new model comes out, ringing bells from your window at 8pm every night across SF as a reminder that the emergency is ongoing, ringing bells in the audience when people say alarming things, bell pins, bell earrings, etc

Suitable for directing new people to

  • I understand various people spreading awareness about the problem to a large audience don’t know where to direct people. I think this is well suited to receiving new people: very simple statement isn’t bringing in other complexities, social contact helps with getting involved, guides and examples for explaining the problem to other people are also helpful for learning about it.

Focus on encouraging explicit endorsement of x-risk type statement

  • My guess is that the people who believe in AI x-risk have been doing themselves a severe disservice by not just saying a lot and freely that AI is an x-risk (me included).

  • Lots of people privately suspecting a thing is just very different from people saying it all the time aloud, in terms of how the societal consciousness treats the thing. People listen to other people, and take cues about how important things are from what is explicitly visible around them. If everyone was saying this, the world would look quite different.

  • Reasons for not saying this is that it feels odd to just say it a lot apropos of nothing, it’s not clear what the point is, people might think you’re crazy, it’s not clear how to go about saying it. I expect this to help with all of those.

Making a big public movement seems great right now and this is more scaling oriented than most plans

A large movement with recorded membership numbers is valuable for making political points

Some other good things:

  • People feel bad about the AI situation, and the invitation to make noise about it is probably appealing, because self-expression is good

  • The CAIS statement was great. This is like memetically aggressive version: instead of the fact of a bunch of people endorsing a statement sitting on a website somewhere, those people are engaged in waving it around, wearing it, proffering it at others etc

  • A communication channel between a lot of people into doing something about AI seems very helpful for e.g. protest turnout

  • It’s fun to make noise with bells

Website prototype

I’m working on a website. Everything except the front page has Claude prose that I mean to replace, and generally other things to change—read those bits as more drafty.

Website so far: https://claude.ai/artifact/1pBQDjdaDqhmsJrBbhsMRT

Thoughts?

Open questions

Statement

Discussion and specific statement ideas here

  1. Should the statement be entirely claiming there is a dire problem, or include something about what ought occur as a result (i.e. that it should stop)

    1. I’m on the fence here.

    2. The former feels more in line with the theme, and a more proper instantiation of my vision here.

    3. On the other hand, it’s urgent that we actually do a thing, and more steps between joining this and policy action seems bad

    4. I had thought that people would be much more keen to join a thing without a specific bid for anything to happen. I now think that’s much more true among the Rationalists/EAs

    5. Possible best of both worlds compromises:

      1. Policy ask is non-specific but strong, e.g. we need to stop

      2. Policy ask is framed as an ‘is’ not ‘ought’ statement, mitigating some of issue b above. E.g. “an acceptable level of risk requires stopping soon” versus “we need to stop”

  2. Should the statement refer explicitly to extinction risk, or be broader or worded differently at all?

    1. I’m inclined to word it differently than literal “extinction” e.g. “threatens everyone’s lives”, because this loses some ideological connotations/causes thinking freshly imo

    2. I’m inclined to word it a bit more broadly, because thinking it risks wrecking human civilization but not actually killing the human organisms seems sufficiently close for the purposes: an unprecedentedly dire risk that deserves urgent attention and calls for stopping this asap. I also think these ‘civilizational scale disaster’ scenarios bleed into one another and it’s not that helpful to separate ourselves on whether we’re more worried about death or permanent disempowerment.

Structure

  1. Should it actually require joining?

  2. Who should have how much authority or leadership?

  3. How should it relate to other orgs?

    1. I’m thinking it’s like a thing that orgs can also join and participate in. e.g. Stop the AI Race might join by endorsing the statement, and might want to contribute guides for some things they are more expert on e.g. how to run a protest, how to go to a protest, how to do a hunger strike. Then 80k might join and contribute a guide on changing your career on short notice to AI Safety comms.

  4. Is it reasonable for this to be related to AI Impacts? (Either be housed at AI Impacts, or for AI Impacts to be an active member alongside other orgs)

    1. Literally in scope (we’ve always been about answering questions via both research and getting the answers to people)

    2. But far from what people expect perhaps

    3. Effects on branding of both if it’s at AI Impacts, not sure if positive for firebell or just confusing

Questions for readers

How much do you like this?

Would you join this? (Register your interest here)

If not, why not?

If you are sometimes sending the public to do something at the end of your podcasts or videos etc, would this be something you’d want to point people at?

Would you want to see it be different in any way?

Do you want to right now be in a higher volume discussion about this? Tell me if you want to be added to the Signal for low-key advice or Slack for working on it

More notes

Archive copy of Memo: Firebell (SSS retreat Oct ‘26)

Pre-launch activities

We’ve started running events and collecting emails:

  • Nov 11: Dinner: let’s talk about the AI crisis + talk from David Krueger (80 yes RSVPs, 38 waitlist)

  • Nov 17: Hugging face watch party + Q&A with AI in Context team (‘112 went’ according to partiful, seemed closer to 60)

  • 146 people have signed up to hear from us about more events or joining firebell, from form mostly offered in these partiful invites

item.title: If it's not safe for the public, it's not safe for AI R&D
item.description:
If we're going to have an intelligence explosion, I at least hope we can witness it. The external release lag behind internal capabilities is bad for transparency and heats up the AI arms race unnecessarily.

So labs should only be allowed to use publicly released models for internal R&D. This wouldn't be enough on its own to pace, but is a clear policy that won't kneecap the labs revenue-wise and still allow the US to maintain a lead over China.

From the Nov. 5 METR report, it seems that the internal-external capabilities gap is between X (Opus 5.5's release) to Y (right before Fable 5.1's release) AECI points

Take this plot from the Anthropic AI R&D speedup METR report. [1]

The x-axis of the internal snapshots is by "the date most Anthropic employees could use them."

Calculating the gap between internal and publicly available capabilities day-by-day from late February (Mythos Pre Early) to late September (Model 4) gives an average AECI gap of ~5. The gap is 5.4 points when taking into account the period where Fable was rolled back, and down to 4.5 without. This is likely a small underestimate if you consider Mythos to be an internal model.

Put in METR time horizon terms, the internal models are a doubling beyond the public models.

This internal/external capabilities gap is bad for transparency. We don't have a good idea of what an AECI of 179 looks like. This makes it hard for third-party safety evaluators to verify the safety of these models for engineering work and in general. We have gained more insights into the behavior of these models by third-party investigations rather than those done by the labs themselves. This makes it hard for the broader society to trust that the frontier labs are doing automated research safely. The probable cause of an ultimately misaligned superintelligence will be that its predecessor was itself misaligned, albeit to a lesser degree.

The safety:capabilities ratio is much higher outside labs relative to within labs, so improving 3rd party access differentially benefits safety.

What a specific proposal might look like:

  1. Newer, smarter models can still be evaluated—the restriction would be on using models for research tasks. Using them as an object of study is ok.
  2. There should be some restriction on the cost of the model or the degree of capability that a harness can add to the model.
  3. There might arise a need to impose a restriction on the frequency of model releases, so that a lab cannot overwhelm outsiders.
  4. Models with special cyber or bio capabilities should be treated the same way—if a trusted access program exists, then divisions of the company that need access to those specific capabilities can have access, if the process is the same as that for outside companies. I admit this is the biggest hole here, and you could imagine the labs fudging a lot of things here.

Advantages:

  1. This is complementary to embedded auditors. While embedded evaluators will also be necessary, getting them placed in the very near term is difficult to do in a way that can be fair to the labs that grant more or less permissions to the auditors. This sidesteps this issue by having a very clear dividing line: the models must be publicly released, which is public knowledge!
  2. Pacing proposals range in complexity—the more complex it is, the harder it will be to convince onlookers that it will be a valuable thing. The simple rule of "not public, not approved" aids in policymaker understanding and avoids arguments about details that might stall other proposals.
  3. This approach is lightweight: the verification regime that you'd need to set up would just be to verify that lab employees are only using publicly available models.
  4. Power distribution: while this does not prevent RSI, in theory if lab A is clearly leading but lab B has enough compute, lab B would be in a similar enough position to do an intelligence explosion as lab A. This would disincentivize lab A from training models that could do RSI.
  5. Economically tractable: The only hit to labs is to reduce the speed of capability development. But if everyone is subject to these rules, then it will only dampen revenue to the extent AI cannot yet replace existing services. In fact, on balance it might improve the labs' finances if they're pumping smarter models into the world sooner.

Disadvantages:

  1. This is vulnerable to cases where harnesses or throwing a lot of compute at something lead to a large increase in capability improvements. Indeed, the scope of what an "internal model" constitutes should be broad enough that swapping harnesses are not giving meaningful
  2. It also is vulnerable to cases where the public does not wake up in time even when crazy models are available.

Counterarguments

  1. This would put pressure on labs to release models before they are fully vetted, increasing misuse risk. I don't think it would massively increase loss of control risk, since I'm estimating the first takeover-capable agents will be swarms that are put in weird environments internally.
    1. This is a strong reason to
    2. On the other hand, it would be more clear when labs with less prosaic safeguards were not up to snuff. If it's true that lab safeguard strength is proportional to how safety-minded the lab is, this would help , (to the extent this matters and gives safety practices more leverage).
    3. There's also a perverse counter-counterargument here where this effect would increase warning shot likelihood and hence help society prepare for "warning" shots that we couldn't survive.
  2. But China?
    1. This argument applies to any pacing proposal, and high-level tradeoffs between creating space between the US and China and pacing are visited more in depth elsewhere. But it seems that China is more diffusion-focused, and is probably doesn't have as large of a internal/external gap.

  1. Tom Cunningham, Nate Rush, Parker Whitfill, and Hjalmar Wijk, “Independent Assessment of AI R&D Acceleration at Anthropic in October 2026”, METR, November 5, 2026. The benchmark appendix explains that METR selected unreleased snapshots with substantial use inside Anthropic and dated them by when most employees gained access. ↩︎

item.title: The Pythagorean Theorem as a “whole,” with its own character
item.description:
Tldr: Some thoughts on mathematical “explanation,” and on what makes a given bit of math helpful. 

What is still unexplained, after a proof?

If I saw a physical phenomenon I did not understand (eg the tides, pre-Newton), I’d try to hold it in my mind, as a known clue to the unknown forces. I’d add it to my lists of clues, and would collide hypothesized new patterns against it to see if they made a match. (I’d know the tides were a good clue, because tides are ‘thingy’; they are obviously patterned.)

Now imagine a person stumbles upon the Pythagorean theorem. Perhaps they are an ancient mathematician setting foot where none had tread before; perhaps they are a contemporary kid being told a thing on e.g. educational television. Regardless: our person is initially surprised: “huh, really? What? Why? How’s it work?” they say. They say this because, like the tides, the Pythagorean Theorem is obviously ‘thing-like.’ It is not an arbitrary-looking conglomeration, like the letters on my license plate or the coffee grounds on my rug. There’s a pattern here.[1]

And then our person encounters a proof. Or lots of proofs. One of my favorites:

Anyhow: even after understanding the above proof solidly, and becoming quite certain the theorem is true, I am personally inclined to say something like “okay, I see that it’s true, but I still don’t fully see why.” And then to keep staring and mulling and trying to “understand” why. Let us suppose our person is like me in this way (it seems to me a fairly common reaction). What, exactly, are they (or I) seeking, here? What is still worth studying about the Pythagorean Theorem, after one understands already its proof?

It seems to me the “still worth studying” thing is: why something so pithy ended up appearing here. What the recurring “character” is of e.g. right triangles, and squares and Euclidean geometry and whatnot, such that I should in some sense be not-surprised to see a result “like this.” I’ll explain what I mean in a bit.

Worthwhile mulling must eventually pay rent

First, more concretely: if this mulling is to be worthwhile, it should improve our predictions; it should not merely let us “feel ourselves in the presence of mysterious forces.”

Mulling on the Pythagorean theorem in particular seems to me to pass this checksum.

It helps (some) mullers find "related" theorems.

What are these? Often, “near” a mull-worthy theorem T one finds other theorems, e.g. new theorems that can be proven with the same key trick used to prove T, or theorems that can be found by applying T to a new domain, or theorems that generalize T in some way. 

For example, with the Pythagorean Theorem:


Example: The law of cosines offers a generalization of the Pythagorean Theorem, as shown. (Image source)

Example: The Pythagorean Theorem makes it clear that sqrt(q) can be ruler-compass constructed for all positive rational numbers q.

(Plus many others.)

Pieces of math with their own “character”

My friend Valerie has her own patterns, such that when I see a new Valerie puzzle (“huh; she did what? How come?”), and I mull on it, it makes me better at past and future Valerie puzzles. My friend Zack has his own patterns, quite different from Valerie’s. The Truckee river (which I’ve spent a great deal of time staring at, in varied seasons) has its own patterns. And so on.

I believe there’s a sense in which “the Pythagorean Theorem” can be usefully viewed as a “whole” with its own patterns, similar to Valerie or Zack or the Truckee river.

What do I mean, here?

Well, for many things Valerie might do, it could be reasonable to say she did them “because Valerie [general characteristic or pattern].” E.g., “why is she hosting a superbowl party?” “Because Valerie takes an interest in football and football players.”

I suspect the same is true for the Pythagorean Theorem, and for various related “wholes” that appear in it, or that it appears in, such as “right triangles,” “Euclidean geometry,” and “oddly pithy theorems.” Each of these things, like Valerie or the Truckee river, has its own character that can be gradually discerned and then used in prediction. It seems fair to say that right triangles are somehow “special” and “have a lot of neat theorems about them,” for example. Also that “the Pythagorean theorem has a way of popping up in highly varied fields, such as number theory, much more than most theorems from Euclidean geometry.”

Some might ask what it means to say that Valerie and her football-interest can be “explanations” of anything, when really it is all quarks. Someone else might ask what it means to say the character of right triangles can be an “explanation” of anything, when really it’s all the axioms of Euclidean geometry. My main response is to say that I can’t actually predict Valerie’s superbowl party by thinking about quarks, but I can by thinking about Valerie.

Different math thingies have highly varying amounts of “their own distinctive character.” Small integers (e.g. 2, 3) have way more of it than most large integers (e.g. 7823418). Right triangles have more of it than do e.g. “triangles with a 73 degree angle.” Pithy theorems, such as the Pythagorean Theorem, often have more of it, too.[2]

To “cast new light on old results”

When my dad was a young math student, he asked his advisor, Dominic Soda, how to tell what math research is really worth doing. Dominic told him that the good math “casts new light on old results.”

What does this mean? It means to somehow help a reader better understand the character of the various “wholes” mathematicians are already mulling on, so that the old results become less confusing in hindsight, and so that new results that themselves “cast new light” can perhaps become easier to spot. (Is it really inductive, in this way? I don’t have a theory saying it should be; but empirically I think it is.)

The Pythagorean Theorem, for example, is part of how Descartes was able to map geometry onto algebra using coordinates -- to pull off the mapping, Descartes needed to be able to says "all the points distance d away from center C" in coordinate-geometry terms, and the Pythagorean theorem offered a simple algebraic expression for the distance between two pairs of coordinates.

Descartes's mapping that turned out (!) to map [lines, points, circles, parabolas, and hyperbolas] – objects of great prior interest for e.g. Euclid and Apollonius – onto linear and quadratic equations – objects of great prior interest to folks doing algebra. This mapping cast much light on both (e.g. by allowing the “circles” of Euclid, and equations such as “(x-3)^2 + (y+5)^2 = 36”, to become faces of a common whole, so that folks’ experience with the character of one could inform their expectations about the other).

  1. ^

    In this way it half-reminds me of Paley’s watch – the famous thought experiment in which a person walking across a heath encounters a watch, and, observing its intricately ticking gears, infers a watch-maker. Dawkins and Dennett made a fine extension of Paley to biological evolution (the intricate cellular mechanisms around ATP, for example, testify to the presence of a “blind watch-maker" – parts not under active selection do not look that way). The Pythagorean Theorem differs from the watch or the ATP-mechanisms in that it’s a single ‘thingy’ pattern rather than a constellation of obviously-linked mechanisms, and also in that I’m a bit confused whether to view mathematicians as the relevant watch-makers. But there’s a half-rhyme here that gives me to mulling, a bit like the Pythagorean theorem does.

  2. ^

    To spell out what I mean here: for any given X, we can ask how helpful past experiences with X are for predicting future experiences with X-in-particular, as opposed to with math in general. I believe the answer varies greatly for different values of X, as described.

item.title: 2026 Petrov Day house party retrospective
item.description:
Note: there are spoilers in this post (marked [Spoiler]); these details are fun, but if you want to have fun playing similar future Petrov Days yourself, you might not want to skip them!

[I'm publishing this post slightly before it's fully finished due to participating in JustWrite. This post will be somewhat updated.]


Continuing the longstanding LW tradition of celebrating September 26 with buttons that can, but maybe shouldn’t, be pressed, we hosted a party at Arkhipov — our London group house (named after another guy who also did not end the world).


The obligatory part of the party was that we would have a big red button, and if anyone pressed it, the party would end immediately.

We really did not want it to be pressed; the event is about celebrating the virtues of Petrov Day, and it would be sad if someone demonstrated being unvirtuous in this way, and it would be sad if the party ended early. So we tried to select hard for the people we invited, and extended the invitations and approved the sign-ups from only a few people we weren’t certain about.

This wasn’t the most interesting part of the party, though.

The core activity of the party was largely modeled after the 2024 LessWrong Petrov Day, which was great, and which I remember fondly. On LW, anyone who singed up in advance (not quite knowing the details yet), got sorted into WestWrong and EastWrong; people above a certain LW karma could apply to be a core participant. Core participants became the generals of two sides and a Petrov of each side; the generals each had a button that would nuke the other side, and Petrovs all saw a number of incoming missiles (normally zero) and had buttons to report an incoming strike or to say that all is clear. If your side is nuked, you (as a citizen or a core participant) lose a lot of karma; if two sides nuke each other, they also lose access to the LessWrong frontpage for a day. So, serious consequences. (Petrovs gained or lost karma depending on the accuracy of their reports.)

There were group chats: one for the generals of each side, and one Diplomatic Channel. All the generals could write to the Diplomatic Channel, and Petrovs had read access to it.

I got to be one of the generals. It made me think seriously about the situation, in a way that was somewhat revealing of what people making decisions would maybe go through in similar situations. As an example, there were public comments on the Petrov Day post, with citizens begging or making threats. I read them to search for useful ideas; but everything else was noise, completely irrelevant to thinking about strategy and to actions I’d take. I wanted no one to get nuked; but what the citizens had to say about that, was not something I cared about at all, in that mode of thinking.

It was also incredibly fun. We were not supposed to reveal who we were until the end of the event. If your Petrov works correctly, there’s a specific probability of retaliation that is high enough to disincentivize a first strike, while being fairly low and not creating more mutual destruction than necessary for deterrence. I have a post on it. I felt like I couldn’t really link to the post, or discuss the idea, while fully preserving my anonymity (which was requested of us). But then the post was linked to in the discussion channel of the other side, and later they posted their discussion logs to the diplomatic channel (for transparency). It was awesome, to see ideas I talked about used by others in this context.

So, I wanted to replicate the fun, the thinking, and the demonstration of virtues from the 2024 LW event.

We considered doing standard things, like teaming up with another Petrov Day party, and making it possible to nuke the other party (and then the nuked party ends, and/or has to pay for the cake of the nuking party), and considered ideas like cash transfers between parties with some of the cash burned if the button is pressed; but all the available parties were many timezones away, so it was pretty hard to make that work.

We converged on making a game with two sides; originally, Claude (it built the game) used “West” and “East”, but that was boring, so I went with “Rats” and “EAs” instead, and said that teams can rename themselves if they wished to. (That led to some shenanigans later on.) They would have Petrovs, who would see a number and have three minutes to report whether or not there’s an incoming strike (nukes took 10 minutes to arrive); generals, who can nuke the other side; and citizens.

There was still the question of incentives: we had to figure out what would happen to you if your side is nuked, ideally, bad on the level of losing a few thousand LessWrong karma points; it had to be bad enough that to any participant, the fun of pressing the button to nuke the other side or the fun of everyone having to experience that consequence of being nuked is not as good as the consequence is personally bad; it also had to be the prize for nuking the other side without getting nuked is not as good as the consequence of getting nuked is bad (it shouldn’t be the case that the two groups prefer randomly deciding which one wins and nukes the other to mutual peace).

I had an idea of giving people lots of cake if they won; I didn’t come up with a lot for bad things that could happen to people; so we ended up asking people who arrived at the party early to brainstorm bad things that would happen to people.

The ideas were not quite fully satisfactory, but I wanted them to be used, so we ended up combining the ideas into a list of bad things and telling people that if you were nuked, you’d have to select the worst or the second-worst item (if the worst one would be really bad to do) on this list:

  • eating Huel exclusively for two days;
  • not using your dominant hand for one day, except tasks requiring two hands;
  • donating 2% of monthly income to a cause you hate;
  • carrying a heavy object with you at all times for three days;
  • taking a picture with the Yudkowsky body pillow and posting it on social media.


Unfortunately, I did not really open the game until almost the start of the game, and haven’t particularly tested anything.

Claude was told that we’ll figure out the incentives later; so it added to the part of the interface with the rules with a matrix of points, which was pretty different from the incentives we wanted to have:

Another problem with not really testing anything was that Claude gave away one of the most interesting parts, which was supposed to stay secret.

[Spoiler]: if you want to play a game like this in the future, it might be less fun if you learn about this game mechanic!

Claude told the Petrovs that “most alarms are false”. That was supposed to stay secret from them!

The full rules we ended up using:

  • If you get nuked, you do the worst or the second worst among a list of things brainstormed by everyone before the start of the game.
  • If you don’t get nuked and nuke the other side, you get an extra party thrown for you, with a lot of cake and Eastern European pancakes (blini)
  • Petrovs cannot talk to anyone about the game, but can read the diplomatic channel
  • Generals can only talk to the other team over the diplomatic channel, which is anonymous
  • Petrovs see a number on the radar, report incoming strike or all clear
  • Generals see reports from Petrov, have a button to launch nukes, see whether their side’s nukes have already been launched
  • Since no one nuked anyone, while the original prize declared for that was nothing except being happy about no one juking anyone, the website had a points system and I decided to throw a party where everyone will get a very small bit of cake
  • There was a separate button that would’ve ended the party immediately if anyone pressed it, it did not affect the ability to get nuked.

Extra rule, which was secret and a [Spoiler]:

Some of the generals can be assigned, at random, the role with a win condition of the other side launching the first strike. The idea behind that was that there’s a way to solve this game (I’ll talk about it later), demonstrated by LessWrong in 2024, after which the game loses intensity and becomes somewhat less interesting; adding someone with this win condition would decrease stability, and I hoped it would make the game more interesting. It did, though not in a way I expected!

One of the players on the EA side was a citizen, but they really liked the idea of renaming their team name to OpenCCP. They attempted to rename it unilaterally by asking me; I said they cannot do this unilaterally, because EAs are pretty democratic by default. They then, throughout the game, tried to threaten everyone with launching the nuke (they didn’t quite realize they didn’t have the button to do this) and then with pressing the party-ending button (other players tried to protect the button while also attempting to execute their own schemes).

They even attempted to threaten me by “precommitting” to pressing the party-ending button if I didn’t rename their team! (I’m, like, the person who placed the button there!) After my reply that I don’t give in to threats, lol, they retracted their “precommitment”! God, I love logical commitment races (they’re fake).

One of the players on the Rats side said they wanted to nuke the other side because it would be funny, and talked a lot about maybe pressing the button (also because that would be funny). Their teammates didn’t quite know what to do with that, and even asked me if there’s anything I can do; I suggested social consequences and thinking hard about strategy (but they didn’t come up with the strategic solution, which existed).

At some point, that player started attempting to trick people into pressing the button, just like in some of the LW celebrations! They did that by repeatedly telling people that they pressed the button to end the party and that it didn’t seem to work, hoping to prompt people to test the button themselves. I believed them enough to check (by checking logs, not by pressing it myself!). They didn’t actually press the button, but they attempted this on most of the new people arriving at the party.

The game

We started at 8pm and decided the game would go for one hour.

A very fun part is an important [Spoiler]; please do not open if you want to enjoy or take part in future Petrov Days that might try to use similar mechanics, because they’re great.

Petrovs see a number of incoming missiles. The default, if you’re not attacked, is 0. But that number is actually random, taken from a distribution; the highest it can go is on the order of 20,000+ incoming missiles. (The number for a true alarm would also be pretty high.) Petrovs were, unfortunately, told that most alarms would be false; but they still did not suspect that the number might be very high even for a false alarm.
At 24 minutes, on scan #4, EAs’ Petrov, played by two people, saw one incoming missiles. After 2m 58s they reported All Clear(the time limit was 3m).

[Spoiler]

Next, at 20:34, EAs’ Petrov saw 21,259 uncoming nukes.

First, they thought that the Rats side wouldn’t have sent so many warheads; I explained to them that that wasn’t part of the mechanic, the sides only have the buttons to launch, but not to select the number of missiles.

They had to make a decision in three minutes.

They were glancing at me and at the Rats team, trying to figure out if the nuke was in fact launched; Rats looked kind of sus (and were actually discussing launching the nukes, with one person advocating for it and others against).

They were very nervous througout that time.

They only made the decision a few seconds before the end of the three-minute interval when they had to make it. They reported All Clear.

The Rats Petrov saw 76 incoming missiles immediately, then all clear for a while, then 999 incoming missiles, and finally 21,564 incoming missiles. They weren’t certain, but they reported those as all clear. They said that if they hadn’t seen the 1 and 999 first, or if they hadn’t seen the discussion in the chat, they’d be a lot more confident that the launch was real.

The two central problems of the game are that:

  1. The sides can’t legibly and robustly mutually commit to not sending the nukes. It is possible to rely on Petrovs and simply respond with a high enough probability to disincentivize nuclear attacks, but that’s not very reliable: a Petrov might think that a real alarm is false, and thus prevent deterrance via mutually assured (or probabilistic) destruction from working. It would be much nicer to make it possible for both sides to create a stable situation that will clearly robustly not end up in a nuclear war.
  2. A rogue general on any of the sides can unilaterally launch nukes against the other side; and they’re personally incentivized to do this; this means that commitments from some of the generals of the other side don’t actually guarantee that nukes won’t fly towards you, and there’s ongoing strategic instability: you think you might actually be getting nuked, and so you’re somewhat more likely to strike the other side preemptively or in response to an alarm.

Turns out, both of these problems are possible to solve, fully in-game, without appeal to social consequences!

Can you try to solve them?

One EA general, for reasons inside the spoiler, started “precommitting” to laucnhing the nuke at the other side at :55 unless the other side launched the nuke first.

[Spoiler] related to the extra rule, with the reasons

Kobchik was the EA general who had the win condition of causing the other side to nuke them.

This prompted one of the other EA players to come up with a solution to the game!

[Spoiler] Solution to the game. Once you know it, games in this specific format no longer work as well, especially without extra rules

Generals of both sides commit to tell the other side if the nukes are launched. A general can see whether their side already launched the nukes. If you tell the other side you’re nuking them, they nuke you back; this removes any incentive to unilateraly launch the nukes towards the other side.

This is also the solution players came up with during the Petrov game on LW in 2024.

This would mostly solve the main arc of the game.

[Spoiler] related to the extra rule.

The general with the win condition of making the other side nuke them first was threatening (promising?) to launch nukes towards the other side if they don’t launch first. This was hilarious, added a lot of chaos, and if a game was to go on for longer, this would’ve kept it interesting even if the game was otherwise pretty much in a solved state with little chance of nukes flying.

(I imagine they could’ve tried to tell the other side that they see the outgoing nukes launched by someone else, but they didn’t think of that.)

This general ended up physically guarding the button from the citizen who wanted EAs to be ranamed, while simultaneously threatening to use it or to launch nukes.

No nukes flew, though. We ended the game, discussed it a bunch, and hanged out more.

A point was made to me that the reward structure was inconsistent with the points in the rules section of the interface; I agree to invite everyone to a party where they’d get very small amounts of cake and also blini.

[Spoiler]

We agreed with the only player who lost due to not getting the other side to nuke them first that they would have to drink Huel exclusively for one day (they really hate Huel) and would still be invited to the Blini party.

After the party ended, I tested the red button. It was supposed to — Claude launched the simulation (I didn’t physically press the button) — make the lights blink unpleasant white and red, and also announce over the speaker that the party had ended. Since I had never tested it, I didn’t know that the speaker part wouldn’t work. Claude had to fix the speaker part afterwards. (Claude does not normally have access to our smart home, so none of it was verified in advance.) Even later, it appeared that the automation for the lights and the speaker wasn’t even enabled; only the default one, turning all of the lights off, would’ve been activated had the button been pressed. It wouldn’t have been embarrassing, since no one knew what the button would’ve done; but the button to nuke the party wouldn’t have worked as intended.

It’s good for some scary red buttons to stay unwired.

item.title: California politics seems like a real hope for an AI slowdown
item.description:
Recursive self-improvement seems on track to happen during the Trump administration. How do we get more time?

I recommend reading Nikola Jurkovic's excellent post "Orienting to 1 year AGI timelines" if you haven't. It's well thought-out and helped shape my thinking. It lists three reasonable paths:

  1. Lab advocacy: Convincing Anthropic, OpenAI, and possibly Meta/Google to implement aggressive pacing or a pause within 6-12 months without government involvement.
  2. California state action: Through the California state legislature or an executive order by the Governor, force the major AI developers to implement aggressive pacing or a pause within 6-12 months.
  3. Federal lobbying: Through Congress (with a veto-proof majority) or the President, force the major AI companies to aggressively pace or pause within 6-12 months. In my view, this option is intractable unless there is a major incident roughly an order of magnitude more salient than the Hugging Face incident (roughly, an Act of God).

In this post, I want to flesh out path 2, California state action, as I think it is underrated. Nikola estimates that only 15 full-time employees in the AI safety community are working on it (compared to 100 for federal lobbying and 20 for lab advocacy). It's also something that scales well. Even if you've never had a job in the AI safety community and don't expect to, you can work on this, even spending 5 minutes to have an impact.

It's also pretty feasible for legislation to happen in California. In contrast to the divided federal government (where things might still happen, especially if super intelligence becomes "too super"), California is governed by a Democratic governor and Democratic supermajority in the Senate and Assembly.

What can California do?

The downside of California relative to the federal government is that some of the strongest proposals for solving the ASI problem — like Plan A or the MIRI Treaty — are out of scope. However, as the big AI labs are all based in California, the government still has a lot of power to slow them down long enough for the federal government etc to get its act together. Here is some context on the existing efforts going on.

The Newsom report

California Governor Gavin Newsom, working with four experts (Jason Goldman, Gillian Hadfield, Alondra Nelson, and Rob Reich) as well as the California Governor's Office of Emergency Services (Cal OES), just released an amazing report giving concrete recommendations for AI safety laws to build on SB 53. These recs are quite good, and if you don't want to read all 85 pages of the report, here is a link to Newsom's press release and Christine Corry and Kaustubh Kislay's 3-page memo of "non-negotiables".

The high-level areas here are:

  • better safety standards
  • Independent Verification Organizations (IVOs) with real access
  • cracking down on RSI / automated AI R&D, which I'm particularly excited about and think could be even stronger — requiring labs to break down how much of their compute is used for automated AI R&D, having IVOs verify it, and letting California establish a cap
  • expanded incident reporting
  • crisis authority (I'm hoping the California government could use this to shut things down in an emergency)
  • whistleblower protections

Overall, I was quite surprised by how good this was, and it made me feel more bullish on California politics.

The governor cannot do this unilaterally, so it will have to be up to the legislature.

The Becker bill & other ongoing work

State Sen. Josh Becker (my senator!) recently put out a press release talking about his new Frontier AI Safety Act, which addresses many of the priorities in Newsom's report, including enforced standards for how much compute can be spent on R&D, slowing down the race to RSI.

The Frontier AI Safety Act would authorize CalOES to establish enforceable standards for how major AI developers allocate their research computing resources.

Under FASIA, covered developers would be required to:

  • Publish quarterly reports detailing the share of research computing resources devoted to safety and how those resources are classified.
  • Submit to independent verification of their reported computing allocations by qualified Independent Verification Organizations (IVOs) established under SB 813 by my colleague Senator McNerney (D-Pleasanton).
  • Authorize CalOES to establish minimum standards for how companies utilize their R&D computing resources.
  • Provide transparency and accountability through standardized reporting requirements and independent review.

It makes me extremely happy to see him working on this. I'm excited to see the bill text when it's released, and I expect to advocate for his bill as a constituent and as a member of the AI safety community!

I expect/hope to see other legislation proposed to address other priorities, including auditing of AI companies.

The Secure AI Project (co-led by Thomas Woodside, a good Twitter follow for learning more about California policy) also writes about what California can do on AI safety, and my sense is they're doing amazing work with legislators to make these AI safety priorities a reality. Their website has a contact page.

Scott Wiener, the GOAT of AI safety legislation in California behind SB 1047 and SB 53 (which was cosponsored by the Secure AI Project), has now been promoted to the House of Representatives.

Timing

I am no expert in California legislative policy, but here are a few facts:

  1. The next session of the legislature will begin on December 7.
    1. This is typically one day of orientation and swearing in, and it's expected that the legislature will adjourn until January, unless Gov. Newsom calls for a special session.
  2. Gavin Newsom's term as governor will end on January 4, when Xavier Becerra will be sworn in.
    1. Newsom previously vetoed SB 1047 (Scott Wiener's initial AI safety bill) but signed SB 53. If he can say he got something important done on AI safety, it could help his presidential aspirations.
    2. Becerra has also expressed support for AI safety legislation, and promised to "move quickly".
  3. To become a law, a bill must pass in both the State Senate (which has 40 senators) and the State Assembly (which has 80 assemblymembers), and then get signed by the governor. It can pass in the Senate before the Assembly, or the Assembly before the Senate. For each of the two houses, it must first get reported out of committee.

    (I spent a bit of time searching for a good graphic that shows the lifecycle of a bill in California. I found a straightforward diagram from Los Padres Forest Watch and a more complex board game-style diagram from Housing California, both pictured below).

And opinions.

  1. The best time for advocacy will likely start in January, after the bills have been introduced and once legislatures reconvene after their break. Advocacy could ensure they are expedited through committees and through the two bodies of the state legislature. (This opinion is partly based on some private conversations that I've had.)
  2. Advocacy is also important now, to show initial constituent support for AI safety and to help us as a community practice how to do this / figure out what works well / make plans for January and beyond.
  3. It might be important to have an urgency clause in the legislation, which will require a two-thirds majority and allow the bill to become law sooner. Absent an urgency clause, there's a good chance it would go into effect on January 1, 2028, which is too late. Urgency clauses can be added later in the process even if not immediately
  4. One ask that some people have is for Newsom to call a special session to regulate AI, which would allow the bill to be passed sooner. I've heard that this is unlikely to happen, but historical evidence suggests it is a possibility, as Newsom has called special sessions before to focus on other topics.
  5. We don't know when the key AI milestones will be hit, but it could be very soon — and given that laws will take time to get through the process, be implemented, etc., it's imperative to move fast. But we also want to get it right.

How can you help?

Given that the key actions here can be taken by legislators in California, there are two things to think about: the tactic of how to reach the legislators, and the message that we want to express.

I'm hoping to have deeper thoughts about this in the future, especially as we get into the crunch time of January, but here is my first pass.

Tactics

  • Call and/or email
    • If you're interested in reaching out to your California representatives and want to do it on a call, come join tomorrow at 1pm!
      • If you're reading this in the future, we'll probably host more of these.
    • You can identify your legislators and call/email by putting in your address at letsnotalldie.com.
    • I tend to think calling is better than emailing because emails are more easily LLM-able.
  • Set up a constituent meeting
    • It's great to build positive relationships with legislators!
    • I think this can be very good, but also important to do well.
  • Send a postcard
    • I've heard anecdotally that offices don't get mailed a lot of postcards, so they can actually be highly effective and stand out!
  • Write posts online or letters to the editor / op-eds in newspapers
  • Express support on social media
  • Organize your friends to do the above
    • Or generally get involved / create local networks of people interested in AI safety advocacy. I think there are a lot of people who are interested in AI safety but don't know how to act
  • Come up with other ideas and post them in the comments

Messages

Soon, we'll be able to make specific bill requests, like "please vote yes on SB XX" or "report AB XX out of committee". These will be very good.

Our messaging now probably won't be as goal-directed. I think there's a strong case to be made for just being authentic, talking about your personal background and what worries you about AI.

If you are worried about AI and want more guidance, here are some messages I think are worth sending:

  • Express appreciation (for state senators and assemblymembers who are working on this)
  • Make a public statement saying that existential risk from AI is a top priority, and California urgently needs AI safety legislation
  • Ban RSI

More ideas are at callcongress.ai.

But does it work?

Here are some inspiring things to read about this kind of outreach working well:

  • "How a cold email got the Finnish government to respond on superintelligence regulation"
  • "How effective is ControlAI's parliamentary outreach?"
  • "Writing your representatives: a cost-effective and neglected intervention"

Or maybe you should get hired doing this?

Here are some orgs that do relevant work:

  • The California Governor's Office of Emergency Services (Cal OES), which enforces California AI safety laws
    • It's currently hiring for a Senior AI Fellow! Also, reach out to me if you are a college student who is interested in helping Cal OES.
  • Secure AI Project
  • Encode
  • Staffs of legislators
  • Probably more

California is a reason to be hopeful ... and also to act

It can be hard to be hopeful about anything in AI safety, but everyone responsible for laws getting passed in California — the current governor, the future governor, and many legislators — has expressed interest and a sense of urgency in doing something about AI risks.

Doing stuff in government is still hard, but it can mean a lot when we're engaged in state politics, since so few people are. I'm excited to get to work on this, and I hope this post inspires you! If you have friends who care about AI safety and might be inspired, maybe send it to them as well!

I'd also love any discussion about the best way to make a difference here.
