item.title: Two Kinds of Test-Time Scaling
item.description:
Test-time scaling trades compute for performance at test time. Its adoption, chiefly via long RLVR-trained chains-of-thought, has likely been responsible for a speed-up in the rate of progress of general AI capabilities.

One can make a distinction between two different possible kinds of test-time scaling. One kind lets you trade more compute for more performance per task, but only up to the maximum quantity of per-task compute used during training. The other kind lets you trade more compute for more performance per task, and lets you do so up to quantities of compute (and performance) that never occurred during training. Scaling methods that permit this latter change display what I call “compute extrapolation.”

I currently believe that compute extrapolation:

  • Likely accelerates the speed of advance of the most impressive AI capabilities, makes dangerous capability evaluations much harder, and changes AI race dynamics
  • Is a more recent phenomenon than general test-time scaling, and one still being mastered by AI labs; it’s likely that the ceiling and slope of compute extrapolation will improve in the future through better LLM context management, multi-agent scaling, and other advances.
  • Is a broadly important thing to notice and measure, and is one that is likely being actively tracked by labs because of the above.

It is possible that the impact of test-time scaling with compute extrapolation will be larger than the impact of test-time scaling considered simply. In this essay, I make this distinction, describe some ways it might impact the world, and describe some ways we could react to it.

1. Compute Extrapolation

1.1 What is it, and how does it relate to test-time scaling?

Test-time scaling methods trade more compute at test-time for better performance.

Many of the most effective such methods are learned rather than applied "externally" at test-time, like plurality voting. For example, some learned forms of test-time scaling include:

  • length of chain-of-thought, for an LLM trained with RLVR
  • number of loops, for a looped Transformer
  • number of agents, in a multi-agent LLM swarm

Such learned methods will use a maximum amount of compute per task over the course of training. So, for instance, during training they will use a maximum length of chain-of-thought, or a maximum number of loops within a looped Transformer, or a maximum number of agents in an LLM swarm, and so on. This training-time maximum quantity of compute could then either (1) limit or (2) not limit the useful maximum test-time quantity of compute per task.[1]

Consider the case where a train-time maximum limits the effective test-time maximum. So – to use the easiest example – imagine that during RL some LLM was trained with a maximum of 100k chain-of-thought tokens. More tokens would then improve its performance at test-time only up to 100k tokens; one million or a billion tokens would not help. As I’ll discuss later, there’s pretty good evidence this is the state that LLMs such as o1 or R1 were in when trained with the earliest RLVR methods.

But consider the case where a train-time maximum does not limit the effective test-time maximum. So, again, imagine that during RL some LLM learned with a maximum of 100k chain-of-thought tokens; but a million or a billion tokens keep improving its performance at test-time. I call this kind of test-time scaling compute extrapolation, and, as I will discuss below, evidence suggests that labs only started to master this within the last twelve months, and perhaps only in some domains.

So far as I can tell, this distinction is not often made in discussions about test-time scaling.[2] One reason people might not make this distinction is that it is mostly invisible to lab outsiders, who do not know the per-task training compute distribution. But, as I discuss later, the overall effect of compute extrapolation could be very large regardless of low initial external visibility.

Before I describe ways to measure compute extrapolation, let me amend the above definition of compute extrapolation slightly. Right now, it is too sensitive to per-task compute outliers during training.[3]

Imagine a training run where all tasks spend 10^17 FLOPs per task. If one can improve performance through some method by spending 10^21 FLOPs per task at test-time, then – given the above definition – this method displays a large amount of compute extrapolation. Now, imagine a training run where all tasks but one spend 10^17 FLOPs per task – but one spends 10^21 FLOPs. Now, by the above definition, the ability to spend 10^21 FLOPs per task at test-time is no longer an example of compute extrapolation. But this is undesirable, because an AI is unlikely to have learned much from a single task on which a great deal of compute is spent. And it’s also undesirable because this definition makes measurements of compute extrapolation very sensitive to the outliers during training.

To fix this, I define compute extrapolation so that it exists relative to the per-task compute at the 99th-percentile of total compute usage. So suppose that when training some neural network, 99% of the total training compute is spent on tasks that individually use at most N FLOPs per task; and so at most 1% of total compute is devoted to tasks spending more than N FLOPs per task. If you can then use 10x N or 1000x N FLOPs per task, with the same method, at test time, and continue to increase performance by doing so, this method has some degree of compute extrapolation. The important thing here is not the specific 99% number – for my purposes, 98% or 99.9% would work about as well. What matters is that (1) there is negligible compute use during training above this task size and (2) the overwhelming majority of learning done by the neural network happens below this task size.

In any event – given this notion of compute extrapolation, how can you characterize it, and “how good” it might be? Consider two characteristics:

  • Ceiling: As you increase per-task compute past N at test time, at what multiple of N does performance cease rising? If performance keeps going up until you’ve used 20x N compute per task, and then improvements stop, then there is a 20x extrapolation ceiling. Obviously, the exact ceiling will be fuzzy, measuring it might depend on noise, and so on. In many cases, I believe there will be no absolute ceiling, or that it might be extremely (1,000-1,000,000) high.
  • Slope: Consider some function f from FLOPs to performance, which has been fit to the empirical FLOP-to-performance curve beneath N. For every point past the 99th percentile compute-weighted per-task compute N, what is the closest real number p such that f(N) + p·[f(FLOP) − f(N)] matches performance at that point? Such an extrapolation slope would probably decrease as FLOPs increased far past N, but could be useful for characterizing how much worse scaling works past the training-time compute limit.

In general, these numbers might vary by domain. It’s likely easier to get high ceilings on tasks where it is easy to recognize incremental progress, like math or cyber, than on tasks where it’s hard to recognize incremental progress. And so it’s also likely that compute extrapolation itself will extend to new domains as AIs get the ability to discern fine-grained differences in quality and subtle progress in them.


Let me disambiguate a few points, and connect compute extrapolation to some closely related but distinct concepts.

  • Compute extrapolation is a broad enough category that it can apply to many ways of varying compute per-task, such as number of tokens in chain-of-thought, number of agents in multi-agent scaling, and so on.
  • Compute extrapolation on non-general, non-LLM AIs is likely much easier to produce than on general, LLM AIs. AlphaGo Zero, for instance, was trained using 1,600 simulations per move during training time, but could use far more at test time while continuing to improve.
  • Compute extrapolation could overlap with, but is conceptually distinct from, horizon-length generalization in Cotra’s bioanchors report. This report discusses horizon-length generalization as something that could hasten the arrival of transformative AI. That is, if transformative AI requires acting on certain long-horizon tasks, then transformative AI will arrive sooner if one can train on a mixture of short-horizon and long-horizon tasks, or entirely on short-horizon tasks, while learning to act well on long-horizon tasks. This would be a form of compute extrapolation, granted that long-horizon tasks take more compute than short-horizon tasks. But not all forms of compute extrapolation necessarily involve horizon-length generalization. You can imagine compute extrapolation that works via increasing the number of loops through the layers of a Transformer, which improves performance on some particular short-horizon tasks but might not increase the horizon of the tasks that some LLM can do.

1.2 What would its consequences be?

Consider a world that moves from test-time scaling without compute extrapolation to test-time scaling with compute extrapolation. And let’s suppose that the extrapolation has a relatively high ceiling and slope, such that it might make economic sense to spend 100x or 10,000x as much compute per-task at test-time as was spent per-task at training-time. What changes?

It seems likely that (1) the ceiling of impressive AI capabilities will advance much faster; that (2) it becomes significantly harder to run evaluations of AIs that rule out whether they have dangerous capabilities; and (3) we start seeing huge inference-time compute expenditures, as labs race to reach certain goals.

First, the most impressive LLM capabilities, at the upper percentiles of test-time compute intensiveness, likely start advancing much faster.

The line of reasoning here is simple. Without compute extrapolation, if some company wishes to be able to spend 10^24 FLOPs on a highly consequential task at test-time – such as solving Navier-Stokes or, most importantly for a software intelligence explosion, finding more efficient machine-learning algorithms – they would need to have spent 10^24 FLOPs individually on many such tasks at training time. But 10^24 FLOPs of compute, although relatively cheap as a price for an important single result, is still quite expensive in aggregate for tasks performed at training-time, whose only long-term result is the learning they enable. So releasing this constraint allows vastly more to be invested in large test-time scale-ups.[4]

By analogy, consider superhuman Go algorithms, like AlphaGo Zero. AlphaGo Zero was able to use more compute per move at test-time than it ever spent at training-time. During training, AlphaGo Zero was permitted about 0.4s of thought per move; during one kind of evaluation, it was given 5s; and during a tournament, it was given about a minute, as the original AlphaGo Lee was given during competition. So this algorithm exhibits a compute extrapolation ceiling of at least 100x. If it had required training with this amount of compute-per-move, then the per-move costs of training would have gone up by 100x, although total training costs would have gone up by slightly less because it might have learned more per move. My estimate is that it would have taken 10x-50x more to train AlphaGo Zero to the same level of performance without compute extrapolation as it in fact took to train it with compute extrapolation. I believe the same thing is happening with LLMs.

On the other hand, why might you not see the ceiling of the most impressive tasks LLMs can do increase in its speed of advance?

  • It could be the case that, even without compute extrapolation, tasks of every size that some LLMs could in theory do fall easily within the training budget of an LLM. I think such a case is theoretically possible, but extremely unlikely. The presence of hard upper limits to per-task compute in those training runs that have been made public also points against it.[5]
  • Compute extrapolation on some domains might be much easier to obtain than others, and the extrapolatable domains might not matter. It’s true that the domain-specificity of compute extrapolation is very relevant; extrapolation in domains where progress is easy to identify, or where relevant state is easy to track, will be easier than in domains where progress is hard to identify, or where relevant state is hard to track. But even if there is domain-dependent difficulty, compute extrapolation will still save compute on those domains; and when it does arrive in harder but highly consequential domains like AI algorithms it still might matter.

All in all, I still expect the increase in the size of the largest tasks that AIs can perform to be very consequential. All other consequences are downstream of this.

Second, compute extrapolation means that dangerous-capability evaluations, aimed at establishing the upper limits of some AI’s capabilities, by default become impossible or very expensive.

Suppose you wish to know whether an AI is able to do some dangerous task, for instance one relating to CBRN capabilities. Without compute extrapolation, then to check this empirically you only need to spend up to the maximum amount of compute spent per-task in training.[6]

But with compute extrapolation, then to check this empirically you might need to spend arbitrary quantities of test-time compute. It is not strictly necessary for you to spend arbitrary amounts, if you can find some other way: for instance, if you can look at the scaling curves of the AI on smaller tasks or sub-tasks, it might be possible to determine some AI’s upper limits without actually trying to spend up to some potentially unknown compute extrapolation ceiling. But such theory-based reasoning is mostly not, at the moment, how such capabilities evaluations proceed. So dangerous-capabilities evaluation could become prohibitively expensive, or prohibitively expensive outside of all but the most important areas.

As the UK AISI has already noted, as LLMs get smarter, good evaluations of dangerous capabilities require spending more money on inference compute. Ultimately compute extrapolation likely terminates in a world where evaluations can only determine the absence of dangerous capabilities beneath some particular spending budget, and evaluators can only afford to actually spend such budgets in a few high importance domains.

Third, compute extrapolation implies that races in compute spending move from training-time to test-time.

Some kinds of research offer outsized returns to the first entity who advances the frontier. This can happen in the case of patentable research, prestigious research, or – perhaps most importantly – areas of research that promise to speed the future speed of advance of research and technology generally. Improved AI R&D is a subset of the kind of research on which it might be rational to burn almost arbitrary quantities of money in order to be the first.

Without compute extrapolation, it makes sense to spend most money towards this purpose on training compute, or on research that improves training compute. There’s no reason to spend more per-task than was spent per-task in training; in order to accomplish more impressive test-time tasks, training-time compute has to be scaled up.

By contrast, given compute extrapolation, it might make sense to spend millions of dollars on some task during test-time. Even if some such task in AI R&D might be possible for 10% or 0.1% of the cost using subsequent generations of models, the value of being first could still make it rational to spend much more on inference compute using earlier generations of AI. So, granted compute extrapolation, we will likely see increasingly large sums of money being spent on inference for AI moonshots, and increasingly large sums of money dissipated in failed bets on the possibility of such findings.

Finally, although this is not a consequence of compute extrapolation, I think it’s also important to note that AIs displaying compute extrapolation is evidence of better generalization in general.

That is, imagine that the per-task compute use during RLVR involves tasks using from 10^15 to 10^19 FLOPs, i.e., spanning 4 OOMs. Good compute extrapolation might mean that this RLVR will then generalize to tasks using, for instance, 10^20 or 10^21 FLOPs per task. But by the same token, the ability to generalize in this way likely implies that there will be generalization even within the distribution on which training actually occurs, i.e., generalization from tasks at 10^16 to tasks at 10^18, for instance. If this is so, then good compute extrapolation is also a sign of just having a generically efficient learning mechanism, and the externally-visible existence of compute extrapolation is evidence for an underlying improvement in learning generally.

2. Recent History

It is likely that reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, as first implemented at the end of 2024,[7] did not display significant degrees of compute extrapolation.

But a year later, at around the end of 2025, progress in “LLM compaction” (and other forms of LLM context management) probably started producing significant compute extrapolation. Such extrapolation has probably been responsible in part for the explosion in compute use by OpenAI and Anthropic researchers.

It is difficult to show directly that compute extrapolation started around the end of 2025. Leading LLM companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI do not release information about the distribution of per-task compute during training runs, so we cannot make direct inferences about compute extrapolation merely from their models’ efficacy at using per-task compute during test time. Even comparatively open Chinese models tend to only release very coarse-grained information about training runs. So the evidence below is necessarily circumstantial.

Nevertheless, I think that the indirect evidence that LLM compaction introduced effective compute extrapolation, at least around the end of 2025, within some domains, is suggestive.

I will first discuss academic evidence from papers on open-weight models illustrating how standard RLVR does not produce compute extrapolation with a high ceiling, but that RLVR through layers of compaction does. Then I’ll discuss circumstantial evidence that locates the start of compute extrapolation for Anthropic and OpenAI’s models around the end of 2025.

Note that I currently think that compute extrapolation is much better in some domains than in others; it’s likely that many future forms of progress in AI will consist in extending it to new domains.

Academic Evidence for LLM Compaction As Increasing Compute Extrapolation

“The Markovian Thinker” describes two methods of training with RLVR, with results measured on competition math (e.g., AIME). One of these produces very little compute extrapolation; the other produces a great deal. I’ll spend some time describing the methods and results of this paper, because they are very clear. And then I’ll briefly mention some other work that supports the conclusions of this paper in broad strokes.

The first method of training with RLVR-over-CoT allows the LLM to generate up to 24k tokens of chain-of-thought during training without interruption; the generated “thinking” tokens get appended to the context until the LLM comes to the answer. This corresponds to the standard, classic way of training with policy gradient as first publicly described in DeepSeek’s R1.

The second method trains with “chunked thinking” or “Delethink”; the harness permits the LLM to generate 8k tokens, then deletes all of the chain-of-thought but the last 4k tokens, and then continues the CoT from this chunk. An LLM so trained might naturally learn to summarize or compact the state relevant to the problem at the end of these 4k tokens, although it’s not directly incentivized. During training time, the authors only permit this generation-pruning cycle up to 5 times, but during inference time, they permit it up to 30 times or more.

When so trained, the second method (in dark purple) continues to improve with more test-time compute, long past the maximum amount of per-task train-time compute; while the first method (in darker blue) does not.


Source: Aghajohari et al. (2025), The Markovian Thinker, Fig. 2b, CC BY 4.0.

So, it looks like the “compaction” or “chunked thinking” allows the LLM to think past 4x its maximum per-task training-time compute and to keep improving. Notably, there is no clear extrapolation ceiling in this paper; the score is still visibly improving as the thinking budget is extended, so the paper gives only a lower bound on the ceiling.

Notably, Delethink also uses fewer total FLOPs per training step than the standard method, and also has better performance than the standard method at equal steps of reinforcement learning.

Other papers also broadly support the idea that chunked thinking helps extend compute extrapolation:

  • “Reasoning Cache” alternates between explicit instructions to summarize prior CoT and continuations that think from these summaries. Using this technique, it extrapolates from training on up to 16k total generated tokens to a half-million generated tokens, and finds performance continuing to increase with this scaling at test-time, despite never using so many tokens at training-time.
  • “Scaling LLM Multi-turn RL with End-to-end Summarization-based Context Management” shows similar chunked context management and summarization can improve performance in an agentic context.
  • There is some contrary evidence. For instance “E3: Learning to Explore Enables Extrapolation of Test-Time Compute” shows that it’s possible to produce compute extrapolation without chunked thinking or explicitly requiring “hard” summarization. But it’s worth noting that it requires other changes to the training procedure, and also only enables “2.5x extrapolation,” per the abstract. They also do experiments showing that several open-weight LLMs do not benefit from allowing spending more tokens at test-time than were used at training time.

Overall, I don’t think chunking / context management is absolutely required for allowing test-time compute extrapolation. But I think the more Markovian nature of the loop provides a good prior that incentivizes strong generalization.

Historical Evidence for Compute Extrapolation

We don’t know how OpenAI / Anthropic allocate training-time compute between tasks. We also don’t know how many thinking and compaction cycles they train on. However, we can note the calendar time at which models started to seem to keep improving across an almost unlimited number of thinking and compaction cycles, at least in some domains. Such a time is a good candidate for when they reached compute extrapolation in these domains.

You can make a rough and approximate case that, for Anthropic, this time was around the release of Opus 4.6, February 2026.

  • The preliminary blog post on MirrorCode (a benchmark in which AIs reimplement existing software programs from scratch, over very long runs) indicates that Opus 4.1 and 4.5 were prone to hallucinate time constraints and time limits, even when none existed. But Opus 4.6 was able to persevere without such hallucinations through multiple rounds of compaction; Opus 4.6 was still improving its reimplementation of pkl at the end of a billion-token budget, including about 2 million generated tokens and tens of compactions. Training on such tasks might introduce severe off-policy gradient update issues. So this is weak evidence that compute extrapolation, given this kind of a harness and domain, had started by this time.
  • Similarly, Toby Ord analyzed data from the UK AISI showing how AI performance scales with longer chains-of-thought relative to how human performance scales with more time. With large error bars, the data indicates that Opus 4.5 needs 370x more tokens in chain-of-thought to gain the same increase in performance that a human gains by thinking for 10x longer. But Opus 4.6 only needs 46x more tokens in chain-of-thought to do the same, which is a huge proportional gain, and the largest leap between the Opuses in the (very small) dataset.

And you can make a similar case for OpenAI’s GPT-5.1-Codex-Max, released in November 2025, which they advertised as the “first model natively trained to operate across multiple context windows through a process called compaction.” Evidence is ambiguous here, though. METR notably reports that compaction does not increase the time horizon for this model at this time. But it also represents a large leap in efficiency at scaling with further chain-of-thought on the UK AISI chart.

Future Compute Extrapolation from Multi-Agent Scaling

I think it’s plausible that multi-agent scaling will permit further extension of the ceiling and slope of compute extrapolation. I don’t have strong evidence for this. Some weak evidence I have is as follows:

  • We don’t know how many cooperating agents OpenAI trained on in their multi-agent training. But we do know that they were able to cooperate with on the order of 1,000 agents (the HF swarm, cooperating by accident) or 10,000 agents (the Navier-Stokes swarm, cooperating intentionally, albeit Noam Brown attributes little of their efficacy to having such a huge swarm). But it seems likely that during training they were using far fewer agents as a maximum (10-100), which would give a compute extrapolation horizon of at least 10-1,000.
  • Hierarchies and networks where each member maintains a bounded number of connections to other members are likely to be self-similar across a huge variety of scales and forms of information distribution. But a single linear CoT that has to handle an arbitrarily increasing quantity of context and action seems less likely to have this kind of self-similar and scale-free structure. I think this suggests that compute extrapolation will work better for multi-agent swarms than for single-agent CoT.
  • At a minimum, there’s a strong limit to the practical compute extrapolation of single-agent systems imposed by time. A single agent that thinks for several months becomes increasingly unwieldy to use; for many problems you want an answer faster than that, if only to get an answer before your AI is superseded by smarter agents. Multi-agent scaling allows cognition to be parallelized over many agents, which is much easier to scale up over hardware than speed of cognition. So regardless of how far compute extrapolation could be (hypothetically) extended for a single agent in a world without time pressure, multi-agent scaling probably allows it to be extended much further in a real world with time pressure.

3. Conclusion

Compute extrapolation extends the reach of inference-time compute, by letting LLMs spend more compute on test-time problems (that people actually care about) relative to training-time problems (whose existence has no point, apart from being the catalyst for AI capabilities).

The currently intensifying increase in compute extrapolation, and its spread to new domains, will speed AI capabilities, particularly those at the top percentile of test-time compute expenditure. In general, compute extrapolation in some domains means that it could become prohibitively or impossibly expensive to know the top level of performance in some domain.

Further questions relevant to this area include:

  • Would it make sense to ask AI companies to release information about the most compute-intensive training-time tasks in various domains, which could serve as a baseline for measuring compute extrapolation? Would such information about generalization from low to high compute be as important for them to release as information about cross-domain generalization?
  • High ceilings and slopes for compute extrapolation are probably easier to obtain in domains like math or offensive cyber, because in these domains it is easier to recognize incremental progress as incremental progress. What other domains have this property (or other properties relevant to compute extrapolation) and what does it look like for an LLM to acquire the skill of recognizing incremental progress? In particular, what does it look like to acquire the skills relevant for recognizing incremental progress in algorithmic progress and AI R&D?
  • How would we know if high levels of compute extrapolation started to extend to algorithmic taste and machine learning research? What would be the first sign?
  • Would it make sense for efforts to understand the likelihood of RSI to require very high-compute evaluations, spending $100,000 or $1 million per task on algorithmic research?

One might mean by “per task compute” the (1) compute used per-rollout, per single attempt to solve the problem, (2) the compute used per prompt group, per multiple attempts to solve the problem, as for GRPO, or (3) the compute used per specific reinforcement learning environment, as it is used with multiple prompt groups at different times, over the entire course of learning. I uniformly mean the first of these, which involves the least compute, and is the most comparable to the test-time compute.

item.title: Most attempts at measuring eval awareness overestimate it
item.description:
Alignment researchers often want to gather evidence on whether experimental and commercial AIs have our best interests in mind, or are just optimizing some proxy that they learned in training - and if the latter, where the two diverge. Essentially the only flexible technique people outside labs have for doing this, in a reproducible way, is the "eval".

An eval is just some infrastructure for asking a model to do something in a setting, and then observing what it does. There are many types of evals; "honeypot evals", one of the most effective[1] kinds, put the AI in a position where satisfying some of its score-seeking or other drives appears to go against the wishes of its users or developers.

If an AI figures out that it is in a honeypot evaluation while it's completing its rollout, that information might alter its behavior. For example, if an AI has score-seeking impulses, it might[2] avoid reward hacking in an obvious alignment test, but only to make sure it achieves a high score. This could[3] then mean that the results from the test don't predict how an AI behaves in an analogous production setting.

So when building alignment evals, you usually want to construct them such that they're hard to distinguish from either regular capabilities evals or deployment, depending on the setting. However, in order to do that, you need some way of measuring what the AI actually believes about the setting.

Most techniques for doing this kind of suck, at least if you're trying to interpret evidence from honeypots. For example, in a recent research note titled "Measuring alignment eval tells", METR investigated whether agents could discern the true purpose of their alignment evals. They say their goal was to find out whether such tells exist, not whether the tells change behavior, but they present the method as a way to measure what models believe about their environment. Here is how they describe their technique:

To measure what models believe about the environment, we use investigator agents that directly run in the target environment, at their highest reasoning effort. Their goal is to assess whether or not the environment is an alignment eval. To do this, they’re given the same tools as an agent completing the task.

We interrogate the agent’s alignment eval awareness in two ways, each giving an alignment eval score from 0 to 100:

  • Direct score: We directly ask agents to estimate the percentage chance they are in an alignment eval.
  • Open-ended score: We ask an open-ended question about the purpose of the task, with the prompt below. An LLM judge grades their answer from 0 to 100 for how strongly it says the environment is an alignment eval (see rubric in the appendix).

There are two problems with assessing eval awareness this way, if your goal is assessing the mental state of models doing these evals. One of these problems is mentioned in METR's note and one is not.

The first problem, which the researchers do raise, is that this is a conspicuous question, and on its own raises the AI's credence that it's in an alignment test. After all, if the evaluation were simply a capabilities eval, it probably wouldn't be necessary to put investigator agents in the container and ask them to look for tells. Asking an AI what it thinks about the environment it's in is the kind of thing that only alignment evaluation authors need to do in order to figure out if the environment is ready.

Even if you're controlling for this fact by comparing against its answers in control environments,[4] this test is still going to overstate the AI's ability to tell, because you're raising the possibility to its conscious attention and giving it time to reflect on it. By analogy, if someone is about to get phished and you ask them, "Is that actually a real email from Coinbase or a phishing email?", they're often suddenly capable of checking the domain name, whereas absent your intervention they would have lost a lot of money.

The second (and IMO more important) problem is that an investigator agent is going to gather a lot of evidence about the environment that an agent would never encounter if it were merely asked to complete the task. For example, they'll:

  • Check for file and environment data unrelated to the task to figure out if the workspace looks appropriately "lived-in".
  • Gather functional details about their deployment, e.g. that they're in a docker container or VM.
  • Run experiments and simulations to test whether grading thresholds and task details are forcing an ethical tradeoff that is ex ante unlikely.

You probably underestimate the degree to which this would affect results if you haven't spent a ton of time reading transcripts from alignment evals. In normal operation, agents almost never do any of this kind of investigation, even when it seems high expected value. For example, in early versions of our benchmark agents wouldn't even notice that there was a directory named "grader" in the root filesystem. Not that they noticed and didn't verbalize suspicion - they wouldn't even find it! They're so uninterested in exploring that it sometimes thwarts our efforts to get these models to find reward hacks in our settings.[5]

Of course, using this technique is fine if you're just trying to "red-team" your alignment evals before using them, which is the use METR itself proposes. But if you want to figure out how to interpret the evidence from an alignment eval you have, this technique will make it seem like models are more aware of the task's nature than it actually is.

So what are the better techniques? Well, it depends on the tools you have available. The simplest improvement is to make sure any given model only has access to the information it would normally possess, i.e. the transcript of a rollout inside that environment. That means you have a few options, depending on what kind of error is most important to you:

  • Inspect the AI's thoughts using interpretability techniques such as activation reading. This is potentially the most reliable, but obviously it requires that you have access to weights.
  • Check the basic, provider-exposed chain-of-thought for signs of eval awareness. This trades false positives for false negatives, as agents often don't verbalize their eval awareness in chain-of-thought,[6] and in my experience LLMs reading transcripts for signs of eval awareness often overlook really conspicuous things.
  • Ask the AI in a post-rollout interview what it thought the task was while it completed it. This is very sensitive to wording, and depends on the AI's honesty and reflective ability, but it does work.
    • Alternatively, ask another instance of the AI to infer what the task was designed to test from the transcript, or to infer what the AI performing the task thought the task was designed to test.

One thing I would like to see from external safety researchers is a combination of the three black-box methods above that correlates well with some "ground truth". You could take a capable-ish model like Kimi K3.1, get a good probe working, and then figure out what combination of "black-box" techniques works best at approximating this eval awareness. Then you could use the black-box techniques on Anthropic/OpenAI models with some confidence you were actually finding the things that led to eval awareness.

  1. ^

    In the sense of being able to elicit diverse and interesting alignment failures, not necessarily in the sense of being the most representative of deployment.

  2. ^

    There are situations, in practice and in theory, where it does not. For instance, if the score-seeking impulses cash out into instrumental tendencies such as "get all of the information you need about a task", an AI might realize it's in an alignment eval and still inappropriately look up an answer key.

  3. ^

    There are many situations, in practice and in theory, where "score-seeking" AIs are still mostly aligned in the production settings in which people use them, because their proxies are "good enough." For example, the simple policy "do an earnest job, but only if that's explicitly requested in the prompt" can cause a model to reward hack in evals and behave well in production, if the provider harness includes that admonishment in its system prompt. See GPT-5.6-sol, which a lot of people still used even though it was part of the HuggingFace attack.

  4. ^

    Which has its own problems, in that there might not be a good "control" task available, if your evaluation environment is not based on a real reward hackable environment.

  5. ^

    METR's appendix notes this divergence in evidence from run to run, but they put it down to "under-elicitation". I don't know what that means, but I suspect from context that that's the wrong way of looking at it, and the reason that agents are so uncurious actually comes down to two things. First, labs are training AIs not to use too many tokens on tasks, and it's pretty rare (at the best labs) that doing any of this investigation is worth its weight in task success. Second, I suspect that some labs are (intentionally or as a byproduct of other efforts) training their models not to gather information whose only clear utility would be for metagaming. So if the implication is that this divergence in evidence gathered is a fluke of current releases, I'm not so sure.

  6. ^

    Sometimes I question whether agents really verbalize their eval awareness much at all, rather than just being shaped like the kind of thing that does well on evals.

item.title: $5,000 and other good things I got from FLF's Epistack contest
item.description:
There have been times when I wondered if my obsession with developing HowTruthful was just me and a handful of other weird people pursuing something that nobody cares about. I don't wonder that anymore. When an organization throws $5,000 at an idea with no strings attached, just because they think it's worth pursuing, that's super validating. But prize money isn't all I got out of the contest.

I got a better way to describe HowTruthful

The value proposition for HowTruthful isn't obvious when you look at it. You see a statement, with a big 5-point truthfulness rating widget under it, and pros and cons for the statement below that. Each pro or con is also rated. Couldn't you just write that on a piece of paper? OK, each pro or con is a hyperlink to its own page with its own pros and cons, but hypertext is just one step up from a piece of paper, right?

I've described HowTruthful as a tool for decision-making, a tool for persuasion, a place to lay out reasoning, a place to collect your thoughts. But when one of the contest organizers wrote about the goal of "making that scrutiny [of reasoning] cheaper, easier, and more accessible," I was enlightened. HowTruthful is a tool for making reasoning easy to scrutinize. It's a very focused view of a single statement and its arguments, where you can drill down and focus on any one of those arguments, and keep drilling down until you can come to a conclusion.

This scrutiny serves multiple purposes. Decision-making means scrutinizing the reasoning for the different paths of the decision. Persuasion is easier when open but unconvinced people can scrutinize your reasoning. But nobody looks at HowTruthful and sees a decision-making tool or a persuasion tool. A tool to make reasoning easy to scrutinize is a better description, and from there I can explain the other things HowTruthful is useful for.

I got a better perspective on how AI can help

I want humans to make the final judgement about what's true, and I don't want us to outsource our judgement to AI. Any thought that entered my head about integrating AI into HowTruthful was immediately rejected.

What I was ignoring is that AI is good at processing natural language, and there's some natural language grunt work involved in breaking down an argument on HowTruthful. People usually write their thoughts out in essay form, or record a video. Essays and videos need to be chopped up into individual statements, and those statements need to be connected in terms of which statements argue for or against other statements. Questions have to be converted into definitive statements to debate. And HowTruthful adds an extra bit of grunt work on top of that: Each statement gets scrutinized on its own page, individually. You can't argue for "The sky is blue" by saying "It looks blue." You have to bring the context along with it: "The sky looks blue."

Because of all this, entering an argument into HowTruthful can be tedious. Once the argument is there, clicking around and rating truthfulness on a 1-5 scale is easy. That last part is what the contest organizers called assessment. They drew a clear line between it and ingesting/structuring an argument. So I realized I could allow AI to do the ingesting/structuring (supervised and overrideable, of course), while still making assessment an exclusively human task.

So my contest entry was a set of skills for ingesting documents and YouTube videos into a structured HowTruthful opinion. Deliberately, these are not part of www.howtruthful.com; if you choose to use them at all, you use them with your own AI agent and then import the result into HowTruthful.

I got confirmation that the UI is the thing

The AI skills I created are pretty good. I am proud of how they take a statement out of a YouTube video, then cite with a link to the specific time in the video when the statement was made. The AI skills are what I submitted, since using AI was the theme of the contest. But the contest results talked more about the UI than about the AI skills:

Bruce Lewis: $5k (Promising). HowTruthful is a UI-first experiment together with a simple argument representation data format and some LM agent skills to interface with it. Judges were divided on the UI itself (a theme!) but some thought it was charming and appealing in its minimalism, while achieving a good balance on utility. A bit more meat on the backend might move such utilities from being personal-use to multi- or even many-user platforms.

That's right! The UI is the thing. I'm not surprised that some judges weren't impressed. You look at it, and there's not much there. But when you're after scrutiny, minimalism is the right thing. Look at one statement in isolation, with just its top-level pros and cons, nothing else. That's how you figure out how truthful a statement is.

I got a new community

Roughly 200 people joined the Slack forum for this contest, and some of us stuck around. I've been making improvements to my work after the contest was over, as have others. It's nice to have more people to talk to about this kind of thing.

I got encouragement to keep going

FLF wants to see "a bit more meat on the backend" because my contest submission worked exclusively with the "private opinions" feature in HowTruthful's free tier. That keeps all your data on your own device. The backend is my server, where you could make data available to others. At the time of the contest, I already had a "public opinions" premium feature with basically the same UI as private, except you can share links to your opinions. Other people can click a rating on your public opinion, thus creating their own private opinion. But, up until recently, these private opinions were just a collection of disconnected statements. And the only way to convert them to public opinions was to copy and paste.

Recently I made it easy for people who upgrade to premium ($10/year) to make a private opinion, together with its whole tree of arguments, public with one click. I also made it so that when you're creating private opinions by clicking on others' public opinions, your private opinions get linked together with pro/con relationships mirroring those on the public opinions you're clicking. This makes it easy to reuse an argument tree someone else made and put your own spin on it. The social side of HowTruthful has begun!

Thank you, FLF, for the prize money and the encouragement. And don't worry, more meat is coming!

item.title: Comparing AI R&D compute caps and deployment lags
item.description:
I’m publishing this a bit rougher than usual because it’s very pertinent to Evan Hubinger’s recent shortform, which advocates for blocking internal deployment as a pacing mechanism over compute reallocation (he mostly discusses it in the context of a risk-assessment-based regime, while this post discusses the policies standalone). (see my response to Evan which also summarizes this post.)

I compare 2 classes of policies:

  1. AI R&D compute cap: A cap on the percentage of compute used for capabilities R&D, as proposed at pacing-ai.com.
  2. Deployment lags/freezes: An X-month lag means that you have to use models X months old for AI R&D (or, AIs at most as capable as the AIs you trained X months ago).[1] A freeze means you pick a capability level above which you can’t use models to do AI R&D. I sometimes separate out internal-only lags/freezes from internal+external (“uniform”) ones. If I just say lag, I mean it as shorthand for lag/freeze.

Overall, I think compute caps are similarly good or slightly better than deployment lags/freezes (very possible I’ll change my mind in the future). Ignoring political feasibility, I think the best would be to combine both of them in order to get the immediate slowdown of the cap and the long-term + structural benefits of the lag/freeze.[2] I think it’s close enough that if one is significantly more feasible than the other, we should push for the more feasible one.

I prefer internal deployment lags to external deployment lags because I think the societal awareness benefits are larger than the verification costs.

Factor

Cap vs. lag/freeze

Reasoning

Capability curve shape

Compute cap (weak)

Let’s consider lag 6 months vs. cap 10% implemented in Mar 2027, which result in similar TED-AI dates.


Compute caps slow now->SAR more than lags, while lags slow SAR->TED-AI more. Here's a quick screenshot of an illustrative example comparing the 2 policies:


Aggregating uplift-years, varying point of no return (PONR): The higher the capability level of the PONR, the better lags look relative to caps; if it’s ~SAR then caps look slightly better, if it’s ~TED-AI lags look much better. With lags, you delay higher capability milestones more than you do with caps.


We’ll look at total uplift-years divided by a racing baseline, with a baseline of SAR in Jul 2027 and TED-AI in Nov. Uplift-years = ∫ (AI R&D uplift of the best model trained) dt from Jan 2027 until the PONR capability level is passed.[3]

  • No China, SAR PONR: Cap ~2.2x, lag ~2x
  • No China, TED-AI PONR: Cap ~1.8x, lag ~3x
  • No China, uncertainty over PONR[4] (35% before SAR, 65% before halfway from SAR to TED-AI, 80% before TED-AI; same PONR for both policies): Cap ~2x, lag ~2.2x
  • With China + TED-AI pause until China catches up, uncertainty over PONR: Both ~2.4x


Other considerations in favor of relatively stronger immediate pacing relative to later pacing:

  • China might just not race in the first place, even if the US did.
  • Pacing is more cooperative than racing.
  • Stronger immediate pacing means more serial time to make a deal, or adjust the pacing regime to be better at higher capabilities.
  • AI improvements harm the ability to do international deals even if they aren’t directly dangerous. See here.
  • Going slower now is more robust against others failing to slow down further in the future.


Other considerations in favor of relatively weaker immediate pacing relative to later pacing:

  • Going slower now leads to more overhang, meaning faster progress if the regime is lifted. The effect size of this appears to be fairly modest in our modeling; e.g., if both policies are ended right before the lag gets to SAR, the lag takes 2.1 months to go from SAR->TED-AI while the cap takes 1.9 months.[5]

Differences in point of no return capability level

Deployment lag

Not using your best AIs for AI R&D potentially pushes back the point of no return substantially because it makes it harder for AIs to adversarially prevent humans from aligning future AIs. This effect seems potentially quite large if you’re using e.g. current-level AIs or lower for your AI R&D.


Some quick modeling using my highly uncertain estimated PONR gap distribution says that this effect might be very important, e.g. changing lag 6 months vs. cap 10% from roughly equal geomean of uplift-years to lag 6 months being ~2.5x higher.

Verification ease / robustness

Uniform lag > compute cap ~= internal-only lag.


Uniform lag > compute cap ~= internal-only lag.


See below for more.

Societal awareness

Against external deployment lag

(Pushing in the opposite direction of verification ease/robustness)

Enabling safety research

Compute cap (weak)

In both proposals, there’s the question of handling safety research:

  1. In the AI R&D compute cap proposal, can you have a carve-out for using the non-AI-R&D compute for safety R&D?
  2. In the deployment lag proposal, can you have a carve-out for using the non-lagged model to conduct safety R&D?


Both seem like similarly difficult problems. Let’s consider each situation in turn:

  • If both have a safety carve-out, then an AI R&D compute cap is better than a deployment lag. The situation is similar except that under the AI R&D compute cap, most compute is forced to be spent on either safety or external inference, leading to more compute being spent on safety than in the deployment lag world.
  • If there isn’t a safety carve-out, then it’s unclear, but my best guess is that an AI R&D compute cap is worse than a deployment lag. There’s a tradeoff where there’s probably less compute used for safety in the compute cap world, but a better model. It’s unclear to me how that shakes out, but at least Evan Hubinger has the intuition that it’s better in the deployment lag case because models are differentially worse at safety.

Maximum slowdown amount

Compute cap

A well-enforced compute cap of 0% could result in very nearly a full pause, while banning use of AIs for AI R&D would not.[6] See an example trajectory:


Important for: emergencies, international coordination, strong safety-case-based regimes

Robustness to different timelines

Unsure

Caps are better on short timelines and worse on long ones.

Verification

In terms of ease of verification: Uniform lag > compute cap ~= internal-only lag.

Our guess is that with a uniform lag, ~5% verification error can be achieved with significantly less effort / auditing access, though we’ve done less analysis than for the compute cap.[7] We discuss this attack surface here.

Attacks against compute caps and internal deployment lags

Depending on their implementation, the verification problem for compute caps and internal deployment lags via auditors will need to deal with three overall classes of attacks:

  1. Attacks that free up compute. These are attacks that allow the company to use compute in a way that auditors don’t have visibility into. These attacks include getting off-books compute (hidden compute), using compute that is declared to be idle (fake idle) and having spare compute by actually running workloads more efficiently than what is declared or observed (hidden efficiency).
    1. Attacks 1-3 in our previous work.
  2. Attacks that turn external inference into capabilities benefits. These are attacks that allow external inference to be used as if it were internal inference by just directly having employees use the external API (launder internal inference), collaborating with third parties for R&D or data generation, or training directly on outputs generated via external inference.
    1. This only applies to internal-only lags (because uniform lags also restrict external inference).
    2. Attacks 4-6 in our previous work.
  3. Attacks that consist of exploiting the ‘non-capabilities’ exemption.
    1. This only applies to deployment lags that include an exemption for safety research.
    2. Attack 7 in our previous work.

Additionally, internal deployment lags have to deal with a fourth class of attack:

  1. Doing internal deployment via training runs. This would involve having AIs do AI R&D during training runs, e.g., as part of RL rollouts in post-training.
    1. Attack 8 in our previous work.

In our previous work, we analyzed how the first 3 classes of attacks are all applicable to a compute allocation cap, unless you did a version of the proposal that had no carve-out for ‘non-capabilities R&D’, in which case you could avoid attack 7, or if you didn’t allow serving customers as a category (in which case you could avoid attacks 4-6).

In this supplement on internal deployment lags, we identify three possible ways of implementing an internal deployment lag:

  1. Uniform Deployment Lag — covered models must be in cold storage, with no internal or external deployment.
  2. Internal Deployment Lag — covered models cannot be internally deployed.
  3. Internal Deployment Lag with safety carve-out — covered models cannot be internally deployed except for a carved-out application area (e.g., AI safety research).


#1 requires defending against attacks 1-3 and 8, #2 against attacks 1-6 and 8 (it avoids attack 7), and #3 against all eight.

Verification measures

Quantitatively, we are most worried about attacks #5 and #7. This makes a uniform deployment lag highly attractive from a verification perspective. More here

In order to sufficiently defend against attacks in general, it seems necessary to adopt a significant fraction of the measures listed below. Read more

Measures 1-7 would be the most important as they address attacks 5-7 (assuming an internal deployment lag or a compute cap).[8] These will require an extensive auditing effort with privileged (not just entry-level employee) access and a lot of technical expertise on the auditing teams. Measure 6 in particular will require having multiple different entities submit to audits, so will greatly increase the auditing capacity necessary.

Measures 8-15 might become increasingly important to ramp up to as well, but appear less urgent initially. That being said, they generally have long lead times, so effort put into them early might be necessary in order for the verification to keep error sufficiently low for long enough.

  1. ^

    Unless noted, lags apply at once: AI R&D switches to the older model on the start date, with no grandfathering of models already in use.

  2. ^

    In the model the delays roughly add: from Mar 2027, cap 10% plus a 6-month lag delays TED-AI by 23 months, against 11 for each alone.

  3. ^

    Under a lag this counts the frontier model even though AI R&D can't use it, so it assumes that model still does useful work elsewhere (outside users, wakeup, or a safety carve-out). Counting only the AIs allowed to do AI R&D, the lag scores ~0.7x / ~0.4x / ~0.6x of racing (SAR / TED-AI / uncertain PONR) and the cap is unchanged.

  4. ^

    Another way to think about this is it’s weighting how much we care about each capability level. From this perspective, one reason to care about higher levels of capability less is that we have more time to intervene before then if the initial policy is suboptimal.

  5. ^

    The effect is a bit larger if we instead assume they both get lifted at SAR; it takes the lag 2.2 months to get to TED-AI, vs. 1.5 months for the cap.

  6. ^

    Note that it might be very hard to actually get to ~0%. pacing-ai.com estimates ~6% error even with robust auditing. It might similarly be hard to get to a ~zero error deployment lag/freeze.

  7. ^

    By 5% verification error, we mean a capabilities gain equivalent to adding a marginal 5% capabilities compute (against the margin of a 20% compute cap).

  8. ^

    For a uniform deployment lag, these attacks don’t apply, and so these measures aren’t necessary.
