item.title: AI Usage Transparency
item.description:
I've updated my blog-post review skill to note how much each post represents me vs AI. On a typical post it's "Claude estimates it contributed 3% of words and 10% of ideas", but when the collaboration had other aspects it tries to detail that as well. Here's what it wrote, dropping the "Claude estimates it contributed":

  • Banana Cases: "2% of words and 5% of ideas."

  • Piercing My Ear for the Whispering Earring: "4% of words and 15% of ideas."

  • Apartment Price Map v3: "13% of words and 50% of ideas; it also proposed and implemented the methodology changes, while I decided which to keep."

  • Transcript: Building an Early Warning System for Pandemics: "2% of words and <1% of ideas."

  • Cheesy Apple Potato Fritters: "2% of words and 3% of ideas."

  • Stroh Violin Talkbox: "3% of words and 5% of ideas; it also designed the 3D-printed adapter, while I took the measurements and tested it."

  • Two New Restaurants on Morrison Ave: "8% of words and 30% of ideas."

  • Reading Speculations Concerning the First Ultraintelligent Machine: "5% of words and 25% of ideas; it also researched details (chess960's history, neuron costs, AI spending) and wrote the marked appendix, while I read the paper and chose what to say about it."

  • Protesting For AI Regulation: "10% of words and 10% of ideas; it also found most of the linked writing on AI risk, while I picked which to include."

  • Ralph Page on Live Music: "1% of words and 10% of ideas."

  • Stroh Violin Shoulder Rest: "5% of words and 5% of ideas."

  • Stroh Violin: "2% of words and 5% of ideas."

  • Testing a Trash Can Faraday Cage: "25% of words and 20% of ideas; it also wrote and ran the measurement software and drafted the methods and results, while I came up with the test, set up the hardware, and wrote the framing."

  • Pulling the Lever in a Subway Problem: "3% of words and 10% of ideas."

  • Lying and Not Lying to Kids: "2% of words and 5% of ideas."

  • Rhythm Stage Setup v5: "1% of words and 10% of ideas; it also wrote ~98% [JK: initially Claude had "nearly all" but I pushed it to look harder] of this year's jammer code, while I designed the setup and decided what it should do."

  • Estimating Our Tail Fire Risk: "1% of words and 40% of ideas; it also built and calibrated the simulation and wrote the marked appendix, while I framed the question and scenarios."

  • Making a Custom Mixer Interface for the 1818VSL: "3% of words and 25% of ideas; it also wrote all of [JK: initially Claude had "most of" but again I pushed it to look harder] the mixer code, while I tested it with the hardware and decided what it should do."

On older posts this is best-effort, and a missing note might mean no AI or it might mean that Claude couldn't find our collaboration session. Going forward, I plan to apply this to each post. My goal is to be transparent about what you're getting, and also track how I'm navigating centaurhood.

For the words Claude looks back over the session transcripts, and credits itself for the portion it originated. It doesn't count quotes or text I've marked with data-ai-generated. For the ideas it's just Claude's estimate, and I pass that along as-is. When it runs into an unusual post I've had it ask me how to handle, suggesting some phrasing but allowing me to suggest my own. This is not going to be perfect, and I'm trusting Claude to estimate its own contributions, but I expect it to be decent.

Claude estimates it contributed 0% of words and 15% of ideas; it also built the system that writes these notes and drafted each note, while I set the rules for what counts.

Appendix

Any summary will elide a lot of detail, so to give an example of how I'm using AI in blogging at this point, here's the full transcript of my conversation with Claude Opus 5.5 in drafting Piercing My Ear for the Whispering Earring:

I've started a blog post at "How I use AI in November 2026", but it's making me think about maybe writing a post "Putting In the Whispering Earring" or maybe "Piercing my Ear for the Whispering Earring" (in reference to Scott Alexander's famous post: https://croissanthology.com/earring)

Thoughts?

Essentially, this isn't something I want in my personal life. But in my work life my org's mission really is a high priority and I want to take the actions that have the best chance of bringing it about. In the near future this increasingly is the centaur model but as AI gets better and better I expect this turns into https://www.jefftk.com/p/teleoperated-humans

I think it's worth writing, and as its own post rather than a section of the November one. The "How I use AI" post is a snapshot. This one is an argument about where things are heading and what you're choosing, and it'll get linked and argued with on its own. A sentence in the November post pointing to it would be enough.

The story fits better than you might expect. In the story, the earring's advice gets more and more detailed. It starts with big life decisions, moves to what to eat for breakfast, and ends with which muscles to move. That's your teleoperated-humans endpoint almost exactly. So you can lay out a three-step path: centaur now, earring soon, teleoperation later. The story already contains the whole progression, so you don't need to argue for it from scratch.

The interesting turn is who the earring works for. Its first piece of advice is always "Better for you if you take me off," and its whole failure is that it serves the wearer's preferences at the cost of the wearer's self. Your position is that at work you aren't the thing being optimized. The mission is. So "better for you" is the wrong question, and you're willing to pay the cost. That's a real and somewhat uncomfortable position. I'd state it plainly rather than soften it, because that's what makes the post worth reading.

Objections readers will raise, which you should get ahead of:

  • Atrophy doesn't respect the work/life line. Can you wear it 9–5 and stay yourself evenings and weekends? The story suggests the changes are physical and cumulative. You should say whether you think the split holds, or whether you're accepting that it leaks.
  • The earring is never wrong; current AI is. Right now your judgment is part of what you contribute: catching errors, noticing when the model is confidently off. That's an argument that putting it in too early actually hurts the mission. So the honest framing may be "I'll put it in as fast as it earns it," not "I'm putting it in."
  • Is independent human judgment part of the mission? For a biosecurity org especially, people might argue that keeping humans who can evaluate AI output independently is itself safety-relevant. You may disagree, but readers will bring it up.
  • Who's speaking through the earring? In the story it's benevolent by stipulation. In real life it's a model from a company with its own incentives. That's probably worth one paragraph.

On the title: I'd go with "Piercing my Ear for the Whispering Earring." Piercing is deliberate and a bit painful, and it's hard to fully undo, which is the point: once your role and skills are rebuilt around the AI, taking it off doesn't put you back where you started. "Putting In" sounds casual and reversible, which undersells what you're describing. "Piercing my Ear" also signals that this is a considered choice and not drift.

One small thing: croissanthology.com is a repost. The story was originally on Scott's LiveJournal around 2012. You might link the original, or both. I'd check the exact URL rather than trust my memory of it.

Want me to sketch an outline, or read the November draft to see where the two posts overlap?

The earring never being wrong isn't actually something the story requires, just something that makes it more dramatic. The end state isn't an infallible AI, but one where I can no longer add value with independent thought.

You're right, and your version is the stronger framing. The bar isn't "the AI is never wrong." It's "when I second-guess it, outcomes don't get better." That's comparative, so it can be crossed while the AI still makes plenty of mistakes, as long as I'm no better at catching them than it is. So the "current AI is fallible" objection drops out. What's left is the question of whether your independent judgment is still adding anything.

That creates some interesting problems the post could dig into:

  • How do you know when you've crossed it? Telling whether your judgment still adds value takes judgment. If you defer more and more, you get less and less signal about whether deferring is right, so you could cross the line without noticing, or think you've crossed it before you have.
  • Atrophy moves the line. Your judgment gets worse partly because you stop using it. So you hit the point where you can't add value sooner than you would have if you'd kept exercising it. That might be fine if the mission gains outweigh it, but it means the crossover isn't purely about how good the AI gets.
  • It happens one domain at a time. You might stop adding value on code review well before you stop adding value on strategy or deciding which projects matter. The earring creeps from big decisions down to muscle movements; in practice it might go the other way, with the small stuff handed over first and the big calls last. That's a nice reversal of the story.

The rest of the earlier list still holds: whether the work/life split survives, who's speaking through the earring, and whether independent human judgment is part of the mission. They fit this framing better now, too.

Maybe "Preparing for the Whispering Earring"? "Piercing my Ear for the Whispering Earring"? I want to talk about how I'm relating to this future and preparing for it, while also being pretty worried about it and not thinking of this as what's happening yet.

I'd still go with "Piercing my Ear," and your clarification actually makes the case for it. Piercing your ear is what you do before you wear an earring. It's the preparation step. So the title already says "not wearing it yet, but getting ready to." It's also a little painful and hard to undo, which fits the worry, and it makes clear the choice is deliberate.

"Preparing for the Whispering Earring" is clearer but flatter. It could also read as "preparing to defend against" the earring, which is a different post.

The risk with "Piercing" is that a skimmer reads it as eager, as if you've already signed up. The opening paragraph can fix that quickly: this isn't happening yet, you're worried about it, and here's why you're getting ready anyway. If you want the worry to be the first thing people see, "Preparing" is the safer choice. But I think "Piercing" plus a careful opening gets you both the vividness and the ambivalence.

I'm thinking of things like moving my todo list from paper to digital, and starting to have it quiz me on what each todo list item means. Having it look over my meeting notes and slack and add todo items.

Those examples fit the title well. None of them is wearing the earring yet. They're building the channel it would speak through. The earring can only give good advice if it knows what you know, and right now a lot of that lives on paper and in your head.

Each example does something a bit different:

  • Paper to digital makes your priorities readable by the AI at all. It's the basic step that everything else depends on.
  • Having it quiz you on what each item means gets the context that lives only in your head written down. "Email Sarah re: thing" means something to you and nothing to the model. This is probably the most interesting one, because it's the AI learning to understand your work well enough to eventually direct it.
  • Having it add todos from meetings and Slack is the first whisper. It's starting to set your agenda, even if you still decide what to act on. That's the small, reasonable-seeming start that the story says leads somewhere.

Some threads you could pull on:

  • Most of this pays off now, with no earring. Better capture and fewer dropped threads help a centaur today. That fits "preparing but not committed": these are low-regret moves that also happen to lay the groundwork.
  • Something is lost with the paper. Deciding what goes on the list, and rewriting it by hand, may be where some of your own prioritizing happens. When the AI adds items, is reviewing them the same kind of thinking, or a weaker substitute? That's a small, concrete version of the atrophy worry.
  • Being fully readable cuts both ways. Making yourself legible enough for the AI to advise you is also what makes you easy to direct, and eventually to replace or teleoperate. That's worth naming as part of the worry.

A structure that might work: the story, then your stance (the mission matters more than your own autonomy, but you're worried and it isn't happening yet), then these concrete steps as what "piercing" looks like in practice, then the worries.

Seems like one important point to get into is that there will likely always be some parts of my work I can't share with the AI, such as information hazards and off the record parts of meetings. So it seems like unless these fall I'm still going to have to think for myself some!

Yes, that's a good point, and it suits your job in particular. In biosecurity, information hazards are central to the work, not an occasional edge case. So the same rules that keep dangerous information contained also keep part of your thinking yours. That's a nice irony to build a section around.

A few ways to develop it:

  • Integrating hidden information may be the hardest job left. If the AI advises you without knowing something you know, you have to decide when that hidden fact changes the answer, and you can't explain to the AI why you're overriding it. That's harder judgment than the work you're handing off. So the protected areas don't just give you leftover thinking to do. They may require your best thinking.
  • Can you keep sharp only in the protected areas? If you defer on everything else, will your judgment still be good where it counts? This is the work/life split again, inside work. Thinking for yourself in a narrow band, under pressure, after months of deferring elsewhere, may not go well.
  • The walls may not hold. "Unless these fall" deserves real attention. Off-the-record norms may erode as AI note-takers become standard. Infohazard boundaries could shift if trusted or locally run models get cleared for sensitive material. You could say which walls you'd expect to hold, which might not, and whether you'd want them to.
  • A gap in the story. The earring's wearer has no private sphere. The earring knows everything relevant. Your version is an earring that's partly deaf on purpose, and it's worth asking whether that's a weakness of the arrangement or what keeps it safe.

This also strengthens the "preparing, not wearing" framing. Even in the end state you're getting ready for, there's a firm limit on how much you can hand over, at least for now.

I don't have the same overriding mission in private, and I enjoy leading my own life there. So I while they're places (like this post!) where I'm enjoying collaborating with AIs, I don't think I would want to wear the earring outside work even if it were perfect./

That's the core of the post, I think. It lines up with the story more precisely than it might seem.

The story's argument against the earring is about the wearer's own good. The earring makes you better off by your own standards, and the story still says don't wear it, because living your own life is the point. You agree, in your private life. At work, though, the point isn't your life. It's whether the mission succeeds. So the story's argument doesn't apply there, and that's why you can hold both positions without contradiction. Your views on the earring aren't really split. You value two different things in two different places.

Some ways to sharpen it:

  • Collaborating isn't wearing the earring. Working on this post with AI is fine because the thinking and the choices stay yours. The AI is a sounding board, not the decider. That's worth stating outright, because it shows you aren't against AI in private life. You're against handing over your judgment there.
  • You may enjoy your work too. If you like the thinking part of your job, putting in the earring at work means giving up something you value, not just accepting a risk. That makes the stance more costly and more credible. "I'd rather not, but the mission matters more" is a stronger position than "I don't mind."
  • The earring would object. A perfect earring would know whether keeping it off in private life is actually best for you, and it might disagree. You've already answered that: you aren't trying to maximize your outcomes in private life; you're trying to live it. The story gives you a neat line for this, since the earring's first words are already "Better for you if you take me off."
  • Will the line hold? This is the same leak question as before. If work is where you exercise judgment the least, does that habit follow you home? You don't need to resolve it, but naming it fits the worried tone.

This might also give you an ending. The post started with you in the earring's world, and it could end with this post itself as an example of where you've chosen not to wear it.

I want to set the scene. How could I describe the state of the art in AI as of Oct. 3rd, 2012

If Oct 3, 2012 is when Scott posted the story, the timing gives you a great hook. The ImageNet 2012 results, where AlexNet won by a huge margin, came out within days of that date. That's usually treated as the start of the deep learning era. So the story appeared just as the thing that would eventually make it plausible was beginning, and almost nobody noticed.

Here's roughly where things stood. I'm confident of the dates to the month, but check them before publishing:

  • Siri had shipped about a year earlier, in Oct 2011. It could set timers and do canned web lookups, and it was famous for misunderstanding people.
  • Watson had beaten Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter at Jeopardy! in Feb 2011, impressively but narrowly.
  • Google's "cat paper" (June 2012) used 16,000 CPU cores to learn, without labels, to recognize cats in YouTube stills. This was big news.
  • Google Translate was statistical and phrase-based, and readable but clumsy. Neural translation didn't arrive until 2016.
  • Go: the best programs played at strong amateur level. Professionals weren't worried. AlphaGo came in 2016.
  • Self-driving: Google's cars had been granted a Nevada license in May 2012, but they were heavily supervised research vehicles.
  • Chatbots meant things like Cleverbot. Nothing could hold a coherent conversation, let alone give advice.
  • Most AI people actually used was invisible: spam filters, recommendations, and search ranking.

A possible way to put it:

When Scott wrote the story in October 2012, the earring was pure fantasy. Siri could set a timer if you enunciated, and the big AI news that summer was that Google had used sixteen thousand computers to teach a neural network to recognize cats. Something that could understand your life well enough to tell you what to do was no closer than a magic ring. Within days of the story going up, though, a neural network called AlexNet won the ImageNet competition by a wide margin, and fourteen years later I'm thinking about how I'd wear one.

You could cut that down a lot. The contrast between the cats and the earring does most of the work.

when did alexnet wih the competition?

[Web search: ILSVRC 2012 results announced date AlexNet SuperVision September 30 2012]

ImageNet 2012 ran to this timeline:

  • Sept 30, 2012: submission deadline
  • Oct 8, 2012: preliminary results sent to participants
  • Oct 13, 2012: full results released publicly. The results were presented at the ECCV workshop in Florence around then.

So AlexNet won about ten days after Scott's Oct 3 post, which makes "within days" a bit of a stretch. "About ten days later" or "less than two weeks later" is accurate and works just as well.

The margin was 15.3% top-5 error against 26.2% for second place. "Won by a wide margin" is well supported.

Sources:

  • ILSVRC 2012 official page: https://image-net.org/challenges/LSVRC/2012/
  • AlexNet paper (CACM): https://cacm.acm.org/research/imagenet-classification-with-deep-convolutional-neural-networks

Anything I should consider in https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/cQkSh9b48WbTaiu2a/sadly-the-whispering-earring or https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/t5psGMdgReuRucEkr/contra-the-usual-interpretation-of-the-whispering-earring or https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/SrSndJwaMHwzY9mLJ/a-market-of-whispering-earrings

[Subagent: Summarize three LessWrong earring posts]

I had the three posts read and summarized. None of them takes your position: wearing the earring at work for the mission and refusing it in your private life. Each one gives you something to cite or answer, though.

1. "Sadly, The Whispering Earring" (Dentosal, Apr 2026) https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/cQkSh9b48WbTaiu2a/sadly-the-whispering-earring

This one is closest to your post: a first-person account of using Claude as a diary and coach, with the author's own rules about what to hand over. They outsource "how to get into doing things," not "what I should be interested in." It's worth citing so readers don't think you're unaware of it, and it contrasts nicely with yours:

  • The author applies it in the opposite place. They use it heavily in personal life, as a coach and for habits, which is where you refuse it.
  • They write "Writing a text like this using Claude would be very wrong." You're writing yours in collaboration with AI. That lets you sharpen the line you drew earlier: collaborating is fine, deferring is what you won't do in private.
  • They're unsure whether this is "training wheels" for agency or a muscle wasting away. That's your atrophy worry, and they also leave it unresolved.
  • In the comments, Martin Randall reports a "willpower overhang" from long use of "Coach Claude." It's a concrete example of side effects you can't see from the inside.

2. "Contra the Usual Interpretation" (AlphaAndOmega, Apr 2026) https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/t5psGMdgReuRucEkr/contra-the-usual-interpretation-of-the-whispering-earring

The argument: if the earring holds a high-fidelity model of you, maybe you didn't die, and the horror depends on a contested theory of personal identity. Your framing mostly sidesteps this. At work, whether "you" survive matters less than the outcome. In private, you care about doing the living yourself, not about whether an equivalent of you persists. Two comments state your position better than the post does:

  • kbear: "if magnus carlsen starts copying stockfish's moves, he will win more games, but he will play less chess." That's your private-life stance in one line, and it's very quotable. It's also your work stance read the other way: at work you want the wins.
  • cousin_it: something that "makes more effective decisions that achieve the same goals" isn't you. They also say how faithful the earring is varies by domain, which supports your point that some areas get handed over before others.

3. "A Market of Whispering Earrings" (mrmoxon, Nov 2025) https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/SrSndJwaMHwzY9mLJ/a-market-of-whispering-earrings

This is short and has no comments. It proposes tests for a trustworthy earring: it "educates the wearer and never instructs," it makes you "more powerful when you take it off," and it's easy to throw away. Your work stance openly fails these tests. You're preparing for an earring that instructs, and mission pressure makes it harder to take off. Naming that directly ("by this standard my plan fails, and here's why I'd do it anyway") would make your post stronger. The post's emphasis on access to your data also connects to your infohazard section: the most useful earring sees everything, and yours deliberately won't.

What I'd take from all three: the kbear quote, a brief link to Dentosal as the mirror image of your arrangement, and an answer to mrmoxon's "never instructs" test. The identity debate is optional, and one paragraph explaining why your framing doesn't depend on it would be enough.

One caveat: the summarizer read the second post's comments only partly word for word. The kbear and cousin_it quotes come from the part it did read verbatim, but check them on the page before quoting.

Fourteen years ago, Scott Alexander wrote the <a href="https://gwern.net/doc/fiction/science-fiction/2012-10-03-yvain-thewhispering\ earring.html">Parable of the Whispering Earring</a>. It's a cautionary tale of an earring that advises you, and to which you increasingly defer as you realize its suggestions are always right.
